a, Characteristics of the two studies. b, Test–retest ICC(2,1) for bilateral, left and right regional volumes (two-way random-effects, absolute agreement, single measurement). Points are ICC estimates. Bars show 95% confidence intervals computed by irr::icc. n = 8 independent participants, each scanned twice (16 scans, paired measurements). Red indicates ICC < 0.4. c, Pearson correlation heatmap of hypothalamic structure volumes and age at MRI in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants (n = 165 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across all pairwise correlations (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). d, Age–volume Pearson r in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants, analysed as pooled (black, n = 165), CBA (orange, n = 91) and AMBR (blue, n = 74) samples. Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across 26 age–volume correlations per analysis. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05, open circles non-significance. e, Associations of age, female sex and intracranial volume with subregion volumes in AMBR, CBA and pooled participants. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients. Bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × s.e.). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in pooled models. Two-sided t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. BH correction covered 26 regions per predictor and cohort. Exact estimates, intervals, t statistics, degrees of freedom and raw/adjusted P are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

Sources indicate that a, Pearson correlation heatmap of extrahypothalamic volumes and age at MRI (n = 458 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across unique pairwise correlations within the matrix (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). b, Age–volume Pearson correlations in the pooled cohort (n = 458 independent participants), CBA (n = 256) and AMBR (n = 202). Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across all 26 regional age–volume correlations within each cohort. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05. Open circles indicate adjusted P ≥ 0.05. c, Forest plots of Gaussian GLM coefficients for hypothalamic (top) and extrahypothalamic (bottom) volumes, ordered by coefficient estimate. Points show fitted coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 316 independent participants in every model, with covariates as in Fig. 1c. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 308 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all eight coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Point color and size indicate adjusted significance. d, Age, female sex and intracranial volume coefficients for extrahypothalamic structures. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in the pooled analysis. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. P values were BH-adjusted across 26 regions separately for each predictor and cohort. e, Body mass index (BMI) associations in AMBR-only Gaussian GLMs. Points show BMI coefficients per SD of BMI and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 174 independent participants in each regional model. Models adjusted for age, sex, cognition, amyloid status, cognition × amyloid status, HbA1c, Epworth sleepiness score and intracranial volume. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 164 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all ten model coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Exact results for all panels are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

a, PCA of 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structure volumes (n = 458 participants). Scatter plots are colored by eight covariates: age, sex, amyloid-β status, cognitive status, intracranial volume (ICV), total brain volume (TBV), study and amyloid days. Three variants are shown: raw volumes (top, PC1 = 44.2%, PC2 = 14.4%), fully residualized for age, sex, ICV, TBV and study (middle, PC1 = 27.6%, PC2 = 13.1%), and partially residualized for sex, ICV, TBV and study (bottom, PC1 = 27.4%, PC2 = 13.9%). b–c, PC1 and PC2 loadings from raw (b) and fully residualized (c) PCA. Bars are red for negative loadings and teal for positive loadings. d, Changes in PC1 (left) and PC2 (right) loadings from raw (orange) to fully residualized (green) PCA, shown as dumbbell plots ordered by magnitude of change. e, Associations of PC1–PC5 scores with nine covariates in raw and partially residualized PCA. Continuous covariates were tested using two-sided Pearson correlations, with r2 as effect size. Categorical covariates were tested using omnibus one-way ANOVA F-tests, with η2 as effect size and an upper-tail F reference distribution. P values were Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)-adjusted across 45 PC–covariate tests separately for each PCA variant. n = 458 participants, with data available for cognitive status in 422, amyloid-β status in 340, CogDays in 441 and AmyloidDays in 358. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. f, Regional volume versus age in n = 181 independent male participants. Each point represents one participant, colored by combined cognitive and amyloid status (black, missing status). Black LOESS curves estimate conditional mean volume. Shading indicates pointwise 95% confidence intervals for the fitted curves, rather than between-participant standard deviations. g, Regional volume distributions after nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching of AD and cognitively unimpaired, amyloid-negative participants on sex and age. The pooled comparison includes 24 AD participants (18 men, 6 women) and 24 matched controls (16 men, 8 women). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Dots represent individual participants, including observations beyond the whiskers. Duplicate outlier symbols are suppressed. h, ROC curves from class-balanced logistic regression with five-fold stratified cross-validation, using 13 hypothalamic subregion volumes or total hypothalamic volume to predict cognitive impairment (n = 422 participants, 140 impaired, 282 unimpaired), amyloid positivity (n = 340, 63 positive, 277 negative) and AD status (n = 316, 24 AD, 292 others). AUCs are mean ± standard deviation across five folds. The subregion model had a higher mean AUC for all three outcomes. No formal comparison was performed. i, Univariate ROC curves predicting AD status from 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structures and total hypothalamic volume (n = 316 participants, 24 AD, 292 others), sorted by descending AUC. The arcuate nucleus (AN; ARC in the main text), fornix (fx), paraventricular nucleus (Pa) and ventromedial nucleus (VM) were the strongest predictors. When lower volume predicted AD (indicated by “−”), scores were sign-inverted before ROC calculation.

a, Donor metadata. The table summarizes condition, age, Braak stage, APOE genotype, amyloid-β status, postmortem delay (PMD), RNA integrity number (RIN) and time of death for each donor. Accompanying heatmaps show donors clustered by pathology metrics (left) and quality metrics (right), with annotation bars indicating condition, time of death, pathology and quality. b, UMAP showing nuclei from this study embedded within a reference atlas of 25 million publicly available human brain cells, colored by major cell type and condition. c, UMAP of the integrated dataset following scVI batch correction, with nuclei colored by condition, batch, individual, and inclusion of the Siletti et al. dataset. d, Boxplots of the per-tissue-sample mean number of genes detected per nucleus, stratified by cell type and condition. Each tissue sample is one hypothalamic subregion from one donor. The center line is the median, box bounds are the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Observations beyond the whiskers are shown as points. CTL and AD contain seven donors each (AD includes the familial case). Young reference samples derive from three donors, except young epithelial cells, which derive from one donor. In cell-type order neuron, epithelial, endothelial, ependymal, OPC, astrocyte, fibroblast, oligodendrocyte, microglia, and leukocyte, n (CTL/AD/young tissue samples) is 21/21/24, 8/4/2, 21/21/19, 19/17/19, 21/21/24, 21/21/24, 21/21/23, 21/21/24, 21/21/22 and 21/21/19. The epithelial samples come from four CTL and three AD donors. These are descriptive summaries, and no inferential test is shown. e, Boxplots of the per-tissue-sample mean UMI count per nucleus, with the same samples and group sizes as d. Boxplot elements are as in d. The y-axis is logarithmic. No inferential comparison is presented. f, Stacked bar plots showing cell-type composition for samples from each hypothalamic subregion (SCN, MN, and ARC). g, Bar plot quantifying the total number of nuclei for each cell type in the final dataset.

Selected significantly enriched Hallmark (top) and Gene Ontology biological process (GO:BP; bottom) pathways from GSEA. The analysis was performed on genes ranked by their signed model weights. The dot plot indicates the top pathways for the all-cell model and for each of the five cell-type-specific models. The x-axis represents the absolute NES, dot size represents the number of genes in a pathway, and color indicates significance (−log10[FDR]).

It has been revealed that a, Top row: violin plots displaying significant DEGs across specific major cell types (endothelial cells, microglia, and OPCs) from snRNA-seq, comparing CTL and AD individuals. Bottom row: boxplots illustrating the normalized log2 abundance of the corresponding significant differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) in CSF, comparing healthy controls (HC) with AD patients. Statistical significance with BH correction is indicated by asterisks (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001). b, UMAP projections illustrating the expression scores for three senescence-related and three NFT-related gene signatures across all nuclei. c, Violin plots comparing the expression scores of three NFT-related signatures across major cell types. Per-sample mean UCell scores for the NFT Orr signature were higher in AD than control (Wilcoxon rank-sum test on 18 AD versus 21 control samples, BH-adjusted across cell types: microglia P = 0.037, OPC P = 0.025). d, Violin plots showing the expression of key senescence-related genes (CDKN1A, canonical; CALR, responses; SOD2, initiators) across major cell types. Pseudobulk edgeR-LRT false discovery rate (FDR) is indicated by asterisks (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001). e–f, Module scores for the mTOR signaling (e) and extracellular matrix (ECM; f) gene sets, comparing control and AD donors at the sample level, stratified by cell type. Scores were computed using Seurat’s AddModuleScore (background-corrected mean expression relative to randomly sampled control gene sets matched by expression level). Each point represents the mean per-sample score for a given cell type (minimum 10 cells per sample). Boxes show median and IQR; whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR. Brackets indicate pairwise comparisons with BH-adjusted significance (Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

According to recent reports, a, Split UMAP embeddings of hypothalamic microglia/macrophage nuclei by group: young, 3,213 nuclei (3 donors), CTL, 24,648 (7 donors), AD, 20,087 (6 donors), and AD_44, 3,472 (1 donor), totaling 51,420 nuclei. In each panel, the full population is shown in light gray and the indicated group is overlaid, colored by inferred pseudotime (top), group identity (middle) or local nuclear density (2D kernel density estimate, bottom). Young nuclei occupy a discrete low-pseudotime region, whereas AD nuclei are shifted toward high pseudotime. b, Group-specific kernel density estimates of pseudotime, with the pooled distribution shown in gray. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Dashed vertical lines mark mean pseudotime: young 1.50, CTL 2.38, AD 2.90 and AD_44 2.12. The distribution shifts rightward from young to CTL to AD. c, Empirical cumulative distributions of nuclear pseudotime. The maximal vertical separation between AD and CTL is the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance D = 0.27, presented as a descriptive effect size. Because nuclei within a donor are not independent, inference used donor-level mean pseudotime: AD versus CTL, 6 versus 7 donors, two-sided exact Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P = 0.0047. Young and AD_44 are shown descriptively and were not tested. d, Group composition of 22 fixed-width pseudotime bins (width 0.2, early to late from left to right). Each bar demonstrates the fraction of nuclei contributed by each group. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and were not tested. The AD fraction increases along pseudotime (Spearman ρ = 0.97, n = 22 bins, two-sided unadjusted P = 1.0 × 10−13), from near-absence in the earliest bins to dominance in the latest bins. A donor-aware binomial mixed model (in-segment versus out, group + (1 | donor), two-sided Wald tests, BH-adjusted across 44 segment × comparison tests) showed AD nuclei were underrepresented relative to CTL in early bins 4–9 (log-OR − 3.23 to −1.28, adjusted P ≤ 0.017) and overrepresented in late bins 16–21 (log-OR +0.62 to +1.31, adjusted P ≤ 0.044), with a single crossover at pseudotime ≈ 2.3–2.9. Exact estimates for every bin are in Supplementary Table 10. e, Nuclear pseudotime by group, with counts as in a. Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Nuclei beyond the whiskers are plotted individually. This panel is descriptive. See c for donor-level inference. f, Top: per-nucleus expression of CSF1R, APOE, B2M and TIMP2 in microglia (same data as Fig. 4f). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Outliers are not drawn separately. Asterisks indicate FDRs from pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests (AD versus CTL, 1 d.f., one pseudobulk per sample, 18 AD samples from 6 donors and 21 CTL samples from 7 donors, BH-adjusted across genes): CSF1R FDR = 3.1 × 10−7 (****). APOE, B2M and TIMP2 were nonsignificant (FDR ≥ 0.05). Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and excluded from these tests. Bottom: CSF protein abundance in young healthy controls (<65 years, n = 38 participants), aged healthy controls (≥65 years, n = 167) and AD (n = 19). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Each dot represents one participant. g, Embeddings of microglial trajectory-associated genes, colored by trajectory rank (left) or correlation with AD status (right).

Recent findings suggest that a, Concordance of AD-associated log2 fold changes between HypoAD (x-axis) and PsychAD dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (y-axis) for genes significant in both datasets (FDR < 0.05). Each point represents one gene. Black and pink indicate concordant and discordant directions, respectively. HypoAD differential expression used one pseudobulk per sample (18 AD samples from 6 donors, 21 control [CTL] samples from 7 donors). PsychAD used one pseudobulk per donor (AD/control donors: astrocytes 313/165, microglia 312/165, oligodendrocytes 312/165, OPCs 313/165, endothelial cells 305/159). Both analyses used edgeR likelihood-ratio tests. Two-sided, unadjusted Spearman correlations: astrocytes ρ = 0.656, n = 87 genes, P = 5.4 × 10−12. Microglia ρ = 0.588, n = 208, P = 9.7 × 10−21. Oligodendrocytes ρ = 0.894, n = 191, P = 1.2 × 10−67. OPCs ρ = 0.978, n = 17, P = 6.1 × 10−6. Endothelial cells ρ = −0.667, n = 8, P = 0.083. P values for OPCs and endothelial cells were computed exactly. The other three used the asymptotic t approximation because the exact algorithm underflowed. Dashed lines indicate zero. b, Age distribution of the 208 donors with microglia in the aging cohort. c, Homeostatic (blue), DAM1 (orange) and DAM2 (red) module scores versus age in the aging cohort (208 donors, 40,226 nuclei). Scores were averaged per donor and then per distinct age. Each point represents one of 64 age-level means. Lines show LOWESS fits (bandwidth 0.6). Spearman ρ and two-sided, unadjusted P values were computed across the 64 age-level means. d, Expression of homeostatic (CSF1R, CX3CR1, P2RY12), DAM1 (APOE, B2M, CTSB) and DAM2 (AXL, CLEC7A, TIMP2) markers in the aging cohort. Left: per-nucleus expression versus donor age, with LOWESS fits (bandwidth 0.5). Right: donors aged <65 years (149 donors, 31,118 nuclei) and ≥65 years (59 donors, 9,108 nuclei). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Asterisks indicate Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)-adjusted P values from donor-pseudobulk edgeR quasi-likelihood F-tests (≥65 versus <65 years, adjusted for sex, BH correction across all 34,176 genes): CX3CR1 3.0 × 10−3, P2RY12 1.7 × 10−2, APOE 3.3 × 10−8, B2M 1.8 × 10−4, AXL 1.1 × 10−2, CLEC7A 4.8 × 10−2. CSF1R (0.22), CTSB (0.26) and TIMP2 (0.51) were nonsignificant. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Log2 fold changes and F statistics are in Supplementary Table 13. e, Age distribution of all 1,040 donors with microglia in the PsychAD AD cohort, including all diagnoses. Panels f and g use the 585 donors with a normal or AD diagnosis. f, Module scores as in c for the AD cohort (585 donors, 112,785 nuclei), computed across 59 age-level means. g, Expression as in d for the AD cohort: young controls (normal, <65 years, 95 donors, 18,764 nuclei), older controls (normal, ≥65 years, 165 donors, 28,330 nuclei), AD ≥ 65 years (312 donors, 63,760 nuclei) and early-onset AD (< 65 years, 13 donors, 1,931 nuclei). Asterisks indicate BH-adjusted P values from donor-pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests (AD ≥ 65 versus older controls, 1 d.f., BH correction across all genes): APOE 6.7 × 10−6, CX3CR1 5.5 × 10−3, TIMP2 1.7 × 10−2. Other markers were nonsignificant. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Log2 fold changes and likelihood-ratio statistics are in Supplementary Table 13.

a, Dot plot displaying the expression of key marker genes enriched in distinct hypothalamic subregions, as inferred by marker from their expression. Dot size represents the fraction of nuclei within a neuronal subtype expressing the gene; color intensity indicates the mean normalized expression level. b, UMAP of the top 30 neuronal subclusters with the highest number of DEGs. c, Strip plot showing log2FC values for significant DEGs identified across all 254 neuronal subtypes. Points are colored to indicate the predominant inferred hypothalamic subregion of the neuronal subtype in which the DEG is found. d, Inferred spatial localization of top AD-altered neuronal subtypes. Visium spots are colored by the predicted proportion of each indicated subtype, mapping transcriptional changes to anatomical space.

Inferred spatial localization of neuronal subtypes. Visium spots are colored by the predicted proportion of each indicated subtype, mapping transcriptional changes to anatomical space.

a, Dot plots showing maximum and mean log-normalized expression of neuropeptide genes and receptors across all hypothalamic neurons (213,469 nuclei from all young, CTL, AD and AD_44 donors). Error bars in mean-expression plots show the standard deviation across nuclei. This panel is descriptive. b, Concordance of AD-associated log2 fold changes between HypoAD (x-axis) and PsychAD dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (y-axis) in GABAergic (left) and glutamatergic (right) neurons. Each point represents a gene significant in both datasets (FDR < 0.05). For each gene and lineage, the result with the lowest FDR across constituent neuronal subtypes was selected. HypoAD differential expression used one pseudobulk per sample (AD versus CTL, edgeR likelihood-ratio tests), whereas PsychAD used one pseudobulk per donor. Two-sided, unadjusted Spearman correlations: GABAergic ρ = 0.028, n = 765 genes, P = 0.45. Glutamatergic ρ = 0.296, n = 301 genes, P = 1.7 × 10−7. Genes are correlation units, not biological replicates. Black and pink indicate concordant and discordant directions, respectively. Dashed lines indicate zero.

Recent findings suggest that a, Ranked bar charts of univariate AUROC for distinguishing AD status using neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores (top) and MRI-derived volumetric measures (bottom). MRI participant counts are as in b. b, Cross-modal comparison of univariate AUROC between MRI-derived volume and neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores for matched hypothalamic regions (1:1 pairing). Left: snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC, with a dashed line indicating equal performance. Right: AUROC estimates for each modality by region, with lines connecting matched estimates. Each dot represents one AUROC estimate, not a biological replicate. No error bars or cross-modal tests are shown. Score direction was chosen so that AUROC ≥ 0.5. The dashed vertical line indicates chance (AUROC = 0.5). MRI AUROCs used 316 participants: 24 with AD, defined as cognitively impaired and amyloid-β positive, and 292 without AD. snRNA-seq AUROCs used donor-level pseudobulks from 14 biologically independent donors (7 AD, 7 control) for ARC, PVH, SCN, MN, PO, TM, ZI and the whole hypothalamus, 13 donors (7 AD, 6 control) for LH, and 10 donors (5 AD, 5 control) for VMH and DMH. c, Cross-modal comparison as in b, with snRNA-seq AUROC averaged across neuronal subregion annotations containing the matched region. For example, AN includes ARC, ARC_SCN, ARC_SMN, LH_ARC, PO_ARC, SCN_ARC, VMH_ARC and ZI_ARC. Left: mean snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC. Right: bars show MRI AUROC and mean snRNA-seq AUROC, and dots show individual annotation AUROCs. Error bars show sample standard deviations (n − 1 denominator) across annotations and appear only when at least three annotations match. Matching annotation counts are 8 (AN/ARC), 6 (Pa/PVH), 4 (VM/VMH), 10 (SCN), 2 (DM/DMH), 4 (MM/MN), 7 (MPO/PO), 1 (TM), 5 (ZI), 3 (LH) and 1 (whole hypothalamus). Standard deviations describe variation across annotations, not donor-level uncertainty. No inferential comparison was performed. All annotations originate from the same pool of 14 donors (7 AD, 7 control), so AUROCs averaged within a region are not statistically independent. MRI AUROCs and participant counts are as in b. AN and DM denote the arcuate nucleus and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (ARC and DMH in the main text).

a, Schematic of the snRNA-seq workflow. Fresh whole hypothalamus was obtained from eight 8-month-old female mice: four wild-type (WT) and four 5xFAD heterozygous (HET). Tissue underwent Dounce homogenization, debris cleanup and nuclei isolation. Nuclei were loaded onto the 10x Chromium Controller, and 3′ gene-expression libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq platform, yielding 60,479 nuclei for analysis. b, UMAP of 60,479 nuclei, colored by major cell type: astrocytes, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, microglia, leukocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, OPCs and fibroblasts. c, Cross-species cell-type correspondence. Heatmap of Spearman correlations between human HypoAD cell types (columns) and mouse 5xFAD cell types (rows), with mouse cell types labeled using transferred human annotations. High diagonal values indicate concordant cell-type identities across species. d, Microglial expression of homeostatic (Csf1r, Cx3cr1, P2ry12), DAM1 (Apoe, B2m, Ctsb) and DAM2 (Axl, Itgax, Timp2) markers in four WT mice (465 nuclei) and four HET mice (912 nuclei). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Outliers are not drawn separately. Arrows indicate the direction of change in HET. Genotype effects were estimated using linear mixed models of per-nucleus expression (genotype fixed effect, random intercept for mouse, lmerTest). Two-sided t-tests used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, with Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment across nine genes. Genotype coefficients (HET − WT, 95% confidence interval) and adjusted P: Csf1r −0.36 (−0.73 to 0.01), 0.073. Cx3cr1 −0.33 (−0.60 to −0.06), 0.037. P2ry12 −0.37 (−0.65 to −0.09), 0.037. Apoe 0.62 (0.44 to 0.80), 1.3 × 10−4. B2m 0.06 (−0.08 to 0.21), 0.36. Ctsb 0.25 (0.06 to 0.43), 0.037. Axl 0.09 (0.03 to 0.16), 0.037. Itgax 0.06 (0.01 to 0.11), 0.037. Timp2 0.08 (−0.12 to 0.28), 0.37. ns, nonsignificant, *adjusted P < 0.05, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Pseudobulk edgeR results using mice as biological replicates are in Supplementary Table 16. e, Strip plot of log2 fold changes (5xFAD versus WT) for significant DEGs by cell type (pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests, one pseudobulk per mouse, four WT and four HET mice, BH-adjusted FDR < 0.05). Each point represents one gene. Representative genes are labeled. f, Selected significantly enriched Hallmark pathways from GSEA of the 5xFAD-versus-WT comparison in astrocytes, neurons and oligodendrocytes. Fill color indicates the normalized enrichment score (NES). Gray indicates pathways not significantly enriched in that cell type. Illustrations in a created in BioRender; Yu, D. https://biorender.com/3747p8b (2026).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Derby County have been one of the surprise packages in the Championship so far this season, but for all the wrong reasons.

The Rams sit 23rd in the table after 16 games with just 10 points to their name, and their misery was compounded after returning from the international break with a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Southampton on Saturday.

According to recent reports, there was a sense of optimism around Pride Park ahead of the start of the latest season. After last term's excellent eighth place finish and the expansion of the play-offs, there was a real sense that Derby could finally have a crack at promotion to the Premier League.

John Eustace had worked wonders since his arrival in February 2025, building a squad that was seemingly capable of fighting at the sharp end of the Championship.

However, with just one win in 14 league matches to start the latest season, the Rams were left cut adrift with Burnley and Preston in the relegation zone, with no escape looking likely.

A much-needed victory over Bolton Wanderers in the final game before the early November international break gave supporters hope that things could turn around, but Saturday's defeat at St Mary's was a depressing thud back down to reality.

Following Saturday's defeat at Southampton, Rams defender Dion Sanderson faced BBC Sport Derby to give his verdict on a difficult run of fixtures ahead, and it's fair to say his words will cut deep for supporters.

"Everything's different, different teams, we prepare differently each week," Sanderson noted.

"But I think from a personal note, it doesn't matter what team you're up against, you've got to play for the badge on your shirt, play for the club, and play for yourself, a bit of pride.

"I think the lads this week, especially, have got to continue [the intensity in training]. We've got to take that onto next week and the week after.

Industry observers note that "We are in a relegation scrap and that's the reality of it. The lads need to start pulling their socks up now, and we're asking a lot from everyone," the defender concluded.

After just 16 games, a player admitting that a relegation scrap is on the cards certainly isn't what fans will want to be hearing, especially after how much optimism there was heading into the season.

After the interview with Sanderson was posted to X by BBC Sport Derby, some Rams supporters reacted to what their centre-back had to say in the wake of yet another disappointing defeat.

One fan remained surprisingly positive, suggesting Derby did enough to earn a point and encouraged the players to keep their heads up.

Another wasn't quite as forgiving, calling Sanderson 'hopeless'.

Another also voiced their frustrations at Sanderson himself, suggesting he should let his performances do the talking rather than post-match interviews.

Finally, one fan blamed club CEO Stephen Pearce for the mess the club right now finds itself in, and suggested nothing will get better until he is replaced.

AC Milan defender Strahinja Pavlovic has admitted that he was a fan of Sergio Conceicao, even if his management was rather totalitarian.

It’s fair to say that Conceicao is a divisive figure within the Milan sphere. The Portuguese arrived and won the Supercoppa Italiana and there were glimpses of the Rossoneri becoming a team under him.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

However, there were far too many incidents which turned most against him – including some members of the squad – and that gave him little hope of continuing. So, when he lost the Coppa Italia against Bologna, he was all but done, if he wasn’t before then.

He’s called it unfair since, but logically there was no way he could’ve continued.

Speaking to the Serbian podcast SS Calcio, Pavlovic admitted that he was fond of Conceicao, despite some of his strange methods, as MilanNews relays.

According to recent reports, “Conceicao banned Nutella, and since then they haven’t allowed it [he laughs]. He was… He’s a good guy, I like him, but he had Hitler-like methods. We go away for a match and at the hotel we split up; the players stay together, everyone else stays outside.

“Knee and elbow pads are mandatory in training, whether the temperatures are below zero or 35 degrees; they have to be there.

“Three days before a match, some players went to a concert until 11 p.m.… He had assistants, or spies if you like, who reported to him, and he made such a circus out of it that in the next match, none of those five or six players were allowed on the pitch.”.

Another anecdote about Conceiçao, when he had just been appointed coach of Milan….

“He was 40 minutes late to the first meeting; all the players and management were waiting for him, and he was in his office. He just wanted everyone to know who was in charge. He did it on purpose.”.

It’s certainly a strong comparison to make; that’s for sure….

5 managers Watford FC must eye up ASAP after Dionisi sack ft ex-Arsenal coach

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Continuing to struggle down at the bottom end of the Championship table, Watford have now taken the decision to sack manager Alessio Dionisi.
  • Following a 5-1 defeat to Cardiff City last month, it was reported then that Dionisi was set to be sacked by Watford, but he held on and dismissed those reports.
  • There had been a slight improvement before the November international break, with the Hornets edging past Lincoln City before earning a creditable goalless draw against Middlesbrough.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Continuing to struggle down at the bottom end of the Championship table, Watford have now taken the decision to sack manager Alessio Dionisi.

Following a 5-1 defeat to Cardiff City last month, it was reported then that Dionisi was set to be sacked by Watford, but he held on and dismissed those reports.

There had been a slight improvement before the November international break, with the Hornets edging past Lincoln City before earning a creditable goalless draw against Middlesbrough.

However, they have returned from the break with a 4-0 shellacking at the hands of Sheffield United at Bramall Lane and that has prompted Dionisi to be let go of by The Hornets.

As a result, we have taken a look at five potential candidates to replace the former Empoli manager in Hertfordshire as Watford fight to keep their second-tier status.

Former Ecuador boss Sebastian Beccacece remains unemployed since leading the South Americans to the round of 32 of FIFA World Cup 2026, eventually losing to Mexico at Estadio Azteca in Mexico City.

Sources indicate that it had been a frustrating time in the group stages for the Ecuadoreans; unfortunately beaten 1-0 by Cote d’Ivoire in their opener before being held to a shock goalless draw by Curaçao. They did then manage to squeeze through with a dramatic victory over Germany at the MetLife Stadium in Fresh York.

Unable to score due to a lack of quality was an issue that plagued them throughout qualification, but a manager’s job is to get a team to create chances in attack and look organised at the back – two things Beccacece managed to do and impressively so in charge of Ecuador as they finished second in CONMEBOL qualification for the tournament, with just five goals conceded in their 18 qualifiers.

A lack of quality in the final third undermined the actual style of football that he had implemented and created with La Tri. He remains a highly-rated coach, and it would be an ambitious appointment for Watford to make but one that may be slightly more realistic after a frustrating summer for the Argentine.

Industry observers note that earlier this season, Parma parted organization with manager Carlos Cuesta after a slow-ish start to the campaign. They have continued to struggle, though, and the lack of improvement, as shown by a 5-1 loss at home to Roma this weekend, only further speaks to the managerial qualities of Cuesta.

Sources indicate that cuesta, born in Majorca, began his professional coaching career as an assistant at Arsenal to Mikel Arteta from 2020 until the summer of 2025. He was poached by expected Serie A strugglers Parma at the age of just 29, turning 30 later in the month after his appointment.

In his debut season as a manager, and such a young one at that, Parma comfortably survived with an extremely impressive defensive record, perhaps to be expected by a duel-led, conservative-focused apprentice of Arteta.

Undermined by big-money defensive sales this summer, such as goalkeeper Zion Suzuki to Aston Villa and centre-back Alessandro Circati to Benfica, Parma were hasty in their decision to move on, fitting of being a Serie A club but a decision that they are perhaps already regretting and could open the door for Watford to find a real coup.

Without much of a playing career to discuss, Edward Iordanescu began his coaching as an assistant, and occasional caretaker, coach at Steaua Bucharest before going on to experience a bit of a journeyman career across Romania.

Iordanescu coached Fortuna Brazi and Targu Mures in 2013 before a couple of years in charge of Pandurii Targu Jiu and then short stints at CSKA Sofia, Astra Giurgiu, CFR Cluj and Gaz Metan Medias before returning to CFR Cluj for the 2020-21 campaign.

Having won the league title as well as a couple of Supercupa Romaniei with CFR Cluj, Iordanescu returned to FCSB, the artist formerly known as Steaua, before getting the Romania job in 2022. In charge of the national team, he led them to UEFA EURO 2024 qualification and even into the knockout stages of that competition before they were beaten 3-0 by the Netherlands in Munich.

His most recent job saw him take charge of Polish giants Legia Warsaw, but he was sacked in October of the same 2025-26 season after an average start to the campaign.

He was heavily linked with the job a few weeks ago and has held talks with the hierarchy, and so his name cropping again would be no surprise, despite his nomadic managerial career.

At the age of 65, it would certainly be a punt for Watford to give Jose Luis Mendilibar his first job in English football, but it would be a real coup for The Hornets should they choose to do so.

Old school in terms of his football values and general tactical philosophy, stereotypically Basque in that respect, Mendilibar has repeatedly got his teams to punch above their weight; be it taking Eibar into La Liga and making them a top-flight stalwart or leading Real Valladolid to a record points tally in the second-tier while reaching the quarter-finals of the Copa del Rey or performing a ‘great escape’ from La Liga relegation with Osasuna.

He was the firefighter brought in to keep fallen giants Sevilla from falling down to the second-tier after a poor stint in charge from Jorge Sampaoli; keeping the Andalusians up and also managing to win the UEFA Europa League, too.

Sources indicate that he then took charge of Olympiacos and added a second European trophy to his cabinet with the Greek giants defeating Aston Villa in the semi-finals and Fiorentina in the final to win the UEFA Europa Conference League. Not able to sustain their best over a season eventually led to his dismissal, but title-challenging consistency is not required at Watford; grit, aggression and intensity it and Mendilibar provides that in abundance.

A slightly different style, but again, looking to Spain for an appointment could see Watford try and poach Almeria boss Garcia Pimienta.

Once one of the more highly-regarded young coaches in Spain, after beginning his coaching career at Barcelona B, Garcia Pimienta led Las Palmas to La Liga playing in a stereotypically Canarian manner, with Las Palmas often referred to as ‘the Brazilians of Spanish football’ and their passing style of football on their ascent was representative of that.

He was eventually poached from Las Palmas by Spanish giants Sevilla, but he was just one of many victims of Sevilla’s decline both on and off the pitch in recent years before rebuilding his reputation across Andalusia and at Almeria.

Pimienta took charge of an Almeria side that had lost the play-off final to regional rivals Malaga in the summer and have massive expectations to get back into La Liga and to kick on further than that with their spending.

Sources indicate that who should Watford appoint as their newly introduced manager? Comment below!

So far this season, they have managed to collect 32 points from 14 matches, sitting five points clear of third place Granada but just a point behind league leaders Castellon, with Pimienta again showing his class and potential outside of the basket case of Seville, where even that now in hindsight looks like a reasonable job.

Once linked with Watford in 2025, could Pimienta now head to Vicarage Road? It wouldn't be a surprise if he was on Gino Pozzo's radar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southampton strolled to a comfortable 2-0 victory over Derby County at the weekend, but what Ryan Manning did in the build-up to the second goal ought to have Saints fans laughing.

Southampton have continued to climb the Championship table with their latest 2-0 home victory over struggling Derby at St Mary's on Saturday, courtesy of goals from Cyle Larin and Divin Mubama.

Despite Derby's insistence on disrupting Southampton's flow, the home side dominated large parts of the game and were deserving of the three points in the end, as Irish left-back Manning has certainly had the last laugh.

It took Southampton a while to really get going in their clash against Derby, with just one shot on target from either side in the first half, making it an extremely close encounter.

However, Eckert's half-time team talk appeared to have the effect the German would've been hoping for, as the Saints broke the deadlock with Larin just before the hour mark, before finally adding a second in the dying embers as Mubama raced through on goal to prod into an empty net following a Derby corner.

With Rams goalkeeper Jacob Widell Zetterström trying his luck in the penalty area in the closing stages, Mubama broke away after Lewis Dobbin played him through on goal, and running alongside the Manchester City loanee was Manning, who turned and appeared to laugh at the chasing Derby defenders.

The 30-year-old, who has developed into one of the best left-backs on the South Coast, has certainly endeared himself to the Southampton supporters since his arrival at the club in 2023, with this just being a fresh reminder of his character and importance to the side.

Manning's contract at St Mary's is due to expire in the summer, and as things stand, he's set to leave as a free agent in 2027.

However, he has made his intentions of staying at the club abundantly clear already, and having become a mainstay under Eckert, it would be a surprise if he wasn't offered fresh terms on the South Coast, regardless of whether a return to the Premier League is secured.

The Irishman will be free to speak to other clubs over a summer move in January, and with just over a month until the winter window, Southampton shouldn't leave this issue unresolved for much longer.

In a recent development, what have you made of Ryan Manning's time at Southampton? Would you like to see him offered a fresh deal? Share your thoughts below!

With Southampton climbing into the Championship play-off picture, Eckert will have set his sights firmly on the automatic promotion places right now.

If it weren't for their four-point deduction at the beginning of the campaign, the Saints would presently sit in 3rd place behind only Middlesbrough and Stoke City, level on points with Wolverhampton Wanderers but with a superior goal difference.

A return to the Premier League is certainly on the agenda in Hampshire, and Eckert will be looking to the likes of Manning to steer his side in the right direction over the course of the campaign.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thomas Tuchel has never been inclined to place much faith in the most famous right-back at his disposal, Trent Alexander-Arnold, once of Liverpool, now of Real Madrid, and – back in an England shirt – still capable of changing games in the blink of an eye.

England always looked likely to defeat a beleaguered Czech Republic team down to 10 men with just 25 minutes played, but it still required one man to conjure the moment of inspiration in this Nations League tie. This was the first cap in 15 months for the right-back now known simply as “Trent” in an England shirt – as well as his Real Madrid jersey – rather than the six syllables of his surname. With the game level at half-time, two minutes into the newly introduced half, he twice won the ball before landing a cross on the head of Anthony Gordon for the first goal.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3 goals in his last 3 games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/xmqPIULJ24.

Industry observers note that will the Alexander-Arnold with England experiment survive? One feels that Tuchel will need a little more to convince him to abandon whatever reservations he has about the Liverpudlian. A week short of his 28th birthday, Alexander-Arnold was winning just his 35th cap. His Real Madrid team-mate Jude Bellingham, a second-half substitute, was earning his 58th cap less than two months after his 23rd birthday. Bellingham was on as captain in place of the man he replaced, Harry Kane, scorer of England’s second. Bellingham’s international career has taken a much less rocky path than that of his Real team-mate.

Having missed the World Cup finals this summer, and had little good fortune around previous tournaments, one wonders if Euro 2028 might be the watershed moment for Alexander-Arnold. Either way, against opponents who sit back, he is lethal when it is time for the big delivery. The Professional Footballers’ Association has leapt to Cole Palmer’s defence following his withdrawal from the England squad.

The union’s CEO,  Maheta Molango, said the Chelsea forward is a victim of a “sick” system that is demanding too much from players physically.

“When England see five players who need to withdraw when the single most proud moment a player has is to be called up for the national team, you just ask yourself, what’s wrong about the industry?” Molango noted at the Fifpro performance summit in London.

“You see people like Cole Palmer, someone who would have played four consecutive summers in a row had he gone to the World Cup, and you wonder why is he missing?”He’s missing because he’s a victim of the calendar and that’s something that needs to absolutely trigger the alarm bells.”.

Man City used ‘sham’ sponsorships in £830m cheating scheme.

Manchester City arranged “sham” sponsorships in a near-£1bn plot to flout Premier League rules, an independent commission has found.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges related to “serious breaches” of the league’s financial rules, with the commission also upholding all but one in relation to their failure to co-operate with an investigation spanning over three years.

The commission found that, of £949.94m City claimed in commercial income over a nine-year period, only £119.25m was legitimate, with the remaining £830.69m illicitly paid by their Abu Dhabi owners.

  • The 48-year-old turned out for some of English football's most historic clubs during a 22-year career, which included a high-profile switch from boyhood club, Leicester City, to Liverpool for £11m in the year 2000.
  • Heskey accumulated 62 England caps and netted seven goals during his esteemed career, as well as winning eight major honours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Premier League, Championship and England international forward, Emile Heskey, has revealed exactly why he opted to retire after a spell with Bolton Wanderers in the mid-2010s.

The 48-year-old turned out for some of English football's most historic clubs during a 22-year career, which included a high-profile switch from boyhood club, Leicester City, to Liverpool for £11m in the year 2000.

Heskey accumulated 62 England caps and netted seven goals during his esteemed career, as well as winning eight major honours.

Having racked up 516 appearances in the Premier League alongside 110 goals and 49 assists, Heskey then returned to Championship level for the first time in 18 years in December 2014 when he initially signed a short-term contract at the Toughsheet Community Stadium.

After leaving Liverpool in 2004, Heskey went on to feature for Birmingham City, Wigan Athletic and Aston Villa, as well as a two-season spell with Newcastle Jets of the Australian A-League between 2012 and 2014.

Returning to England in late 2014, it was confirmed the striker would sign an initial short-term contract with the Whites, who were managed by Heskey's former Leicester teammate, Neil Lennon, at the time.

During his final career stint, he was partnered with Icelandic striker, Eidur Gudjohnsen, who had returned to the North West for a second spell earlier in December 2014, with the latter providing a debut goal for Heskey against Blackburn Rovers on Boxing Day of 2014.

In total, Heskey made 48 appearances for Wanderers, but his only full season at the club and the last of his career ended in relegation to League One, before he became one of 13 players who departed upon the expiration of their contracts.

Heskey started just 15 Championship games in his final career season, scoring twice against Charlton Athletic and Brighton and Hove Albion, but had already surpassed his 38th birthday at the midpoint of the campaign.

There are several examples of one-time top-level strikers continuing to lead the line into their 40s, but speaking to current Burnley forward, Jamie Vardy, Heskey revealed how he knew it was time for him to call it quits on his playing days.

"I went to Australia for two years then came back to Bolton," he mentioned.

"It was basically, in training, more or less, when you see young kids running past you, and you think, not 'I can't do this anymore', because I could've, and I was in good shape and I felt fine, but I didn't want people running past me and not being able to tackle and get back at them like my head was telling me I could do.

"I was like, 'Do I really want to keep going down the leagues to League One and League Two and continue there', just for what?," Heskey admitted.

Bolton fans, did Emile Heskey still impress you in his career's latter stages? Comment below!

Recent findings suggest that "My boys were getting bigger, and I just decided that was enough for me. I got to 38 and probably could've played another one or two years, I think.".

Vardy, 39, is known for his remarkable 200-goal exploits at Leicester, during which he won the Premier League, FA Cup, Community Shield and two Championship titles between 2012 and 2025.

However, he then admitted to Heskey that he has had similar conversations with ex-professionals who may have retired earlier in their 30s, with the Sheffield native still turning out on a regular basis in the second tier.

There are shades between the final club stint of Heskey's career and his own, with Burnley currently in a dire predicament in the Championship after relegation from the Premier League, as they could emulate the unwanted feats of Luton Town and Leicester and become the third team to suffer successive relegations from the top-flight to League One in as many years.

His appointment makes him Manchester United’s eighth permanent manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Pochettino brings considerable Premier League experience after previous spells with Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea. He has also managed Paris Saint-Germain before the USA job.

As he faces Liverpool for his first game on Sunday, the question arises: is he facing the toughest job in the Premier League?

The question was posed on BBC Radio about who is going to have more pressure, Pochettino or Thomas Frank at Crystal Palace.

According to former Premier League defender Nedum Onuoha, the expectations surrounding Manchester United will make the Argentine’s job considerably harder.

It has been revealed that pochettino is preparing for his first game in charge of Manchester United, with Liverpool waiting at Anfield on November 22. However, the challenge facing the upcoming manager goes beyond getting results on the pitch.

Onuoha believes Pochettino will have to deal with constant discussion and criticism about his work, much of it coming from former United players who are now in the media.

Choosing between Pochettino and Frank, Onuoha mentioned, “Probably Pochettino, because every former Manchester United player works in the media, so there will always be discussion around what he is doing.

Sources indicate that “Whereas Frank can just enjoy playing his football at Crystal Palace. If he does well then it is great, if he doesn’t do well then it is still OK.

“But from Pochettino’s perspective, if Manchester United finish the season 15th in the Premier League, whether we like it or not, there will be some criticism of him because he’s had 28 games to do something.”.

Recent findings suggest that the comments just highlight the difference in expectations at the two clubs. Frank may have more freedom to work without the same level of attention, while Pochettino will be judged from day one against the standards historically associated with Manchester United. That is one major problem for Pochettino.

Rory Smith from The Observer highlighted another glaring problem at United. Highlighting a major problem, Smith stated, “there is a cycle element to Manchester United whereby a manager comes in, makes things a bit better, and then within a year to 18 months they aren’t challenging for titles again because the Premier League has changed since they were a dominant force.”.

Recent findings suggest that pochettino’s first taste of action as a United manager will be against Liverpool at Anfield on November 22. That opening fixture will give him an immediate test, but the bigger task will be to get back United to winning ways, step by step.

Industry observers note that will the Manchester United job be without pressure for Mauricio Pochettino? Absolutely Not.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Life after professional football has been a mixed bag for Dexter Blackstock, but the former striker has found himself a new niche in the pharmaceutical industry.

Upon first glance, the post-playing career options of the professional footballer can appear somewhat limited. Coaching or the media are the obvious options, but paid employment in these sectors can be limited, and it might not appeal to all.

But by the time that most players reach their late twenties, there may be decisions that have to be made, and in the case of Dexter Blackstock, a player who built himself a fearsome reputation as a striker with a number of clubs including Nottingham Forest and Queens Park Rangers, the decisions that he did make coupled with his entrepreneurial instincts have led him into an industry that few would have expected while he was playing.

Born in Oxford and brought up in Oxford United's youth academy, Dexter Blackstock had his first breakthrough in the senior game after transferring to Southampton in 2003. First brought into the first-team squad during an injury crisis, he came off the bench at half-time during a League Cup match in September 2004 against Colchester United with the Saints trailling by a goal to nil, scoring a second half hat-trick to help secure the Saints a 3-2 win.

Despite this - and scoring in a hotly-contested Premier League derby match with Portsmouth a couple of months later - Blackstock was unable to tie down a regular starting place in the Southampton team and, following spells on loan with Plymouth Argyle and Derby County, moved on to Queens Park Rangers in 2006.

Industry observers note that blackstock would go on to build his reputation further at Loftus Road, scoring 32 times in 117 appearances for QPR over the next three years. He also made two appearances for the England under-21s during this time, having also played for the under-18 and under-19 teams while at Southampton.

In a recent development, but in March 2009, he was sent on loan to a Nottingham Forest team that was battling to avoid relegation from the Championship, amid reports that he would be going to The City Ground permanently should they stay up. Forest ended the season in 19th place in the table, and consequently his move was made permanent that summer.

Blackstock spent seven years at Forest, with a loan spell at Leeds United in 2013. He had some problems with injuries while he was there, missing a year from November 2010 with a knee ligament injury, but still managed to score 44 goals for them in 187 appearances. And while he never got to play a full international match for England, he did also qualify to play for Antigua & Barbuda and made 12 appearances for them between 2012 and 2016.

He left Nottingham Forest by mutual consent at the end of the summer 2016 transfer window and moved on to Rotherham United, but his spell with the Millers only lasted a year before his three-year contract was mutually cancelled after a year, and he retired from the game at 31 years of age.

By the time that his playing career came to an end, Blackstock already had an idea of what he wanted to do afterwards. He'd built up a portfolio of buy-to-let properties, but his early experience as a landlord wasn't successful.

Industry observers note that in October 2019, he was fined £24,000 at Nottingham Magistrates Court after inspectors found a number of his properties to be in a state of disrepair. He admitted 12 counts of failing to license the properties and was fined £24,000 and ordered to pay £1,100 costs and a £170 victim surcharge on top of his fine. In 2021, he was ordered to repay £8,500 in housing benefit that he'd received for the unlicensed properties.

But Blackstock's entrpreneurial leanings had by this time already taken him in a latest direction. He formed MediConnect with a view towards using blockchain technology to counter the negative image that online pharmacies had received over concerns regarding a lack of controls to prevent the over-prescription of strong painkillers to customers.

According to recent reports, at the start of 2019, Blackstock spoke to The Sun about his upcoming business venture, and also shone a little light on the end of his playing career. “I had lost my mojo and I had no intention of carrying on playing football", he told them, "I wasn’t enjoying playing at Rotherham." On his move into pharmaceuticals, he added, "As it stands, there is nothing to stop anyone ordering drugs from one online pharmacy, then exactly the same with another organization and then going down to their local GP and topping up with the same.".

In 2021, Blackstock spoke to World Pharmaceutical Frontiers in greater detail about his vision. "Anyone who’s using an online pharmacy platform will need a unique customer number and every transaction will be put on the blockchain," he told them, "so the next pharmacy can check whether the patient can have that drug in the same timeframe or mix the drugs.".

The previous year, at the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, he told the BBC that he was using his firm to help the public donate personal protective equipment (PPE) to frontline staff dealing with the pandemic. By 2023, he had a reported net worth of £7.8 million, with The Sun reporting that, "the bulk of his earnings" was still coming "from the 50 properties he owns." If nothing else, the experience of Dexter Blackstock demonstrates that the post-career options for the professional footballer are as broad as their imaginations will let them believe.

Latest Update: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 77 min read (15415 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~77 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies1,2,3,4,5,6,7.
  • Uncontrolled lipid peroxidation is integral to ferroptosis5,15.
  • Potentially relevant immunoregulatory factors produced by ferroptotic cancer cells are oxylipins, bioactive lipids generated through peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane lipids, a hallmark of ferroptosis15.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers1,2,3,4,8,9. Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8+ T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies10,11,12,13. However, ferroptotic cells limit this response8,9,10,14, resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca2+ influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE2 production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE2 production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE2 production or disrupting PGE2 signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8+ T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

Uncontrolled lipid peroxidation is integral to ferroptosis5,15. Cancer cells are commonly protected from unrestrained lipid peroxidation and spontaneous ferroptotic cell death by molecular defence systems such as the system xc––glutathione (GSH)–glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) pathway5,16, in which GPX4 is the key enzyme mediating lipid peroxide detoxification. Strategies to promote ferroptosis by blockade of ferroptosis defence systems, such as GPX4 inhibitors, have been considered promising approaches to achieve tumour elimination in patients with difficult-to-treat cancers8,9. Studies using preclinical mouse models have uncovered that effective tumour elimination by ferroptosis-inducing strategies requires anticancer immunity by DCs10 and tumour-infiltrating CD8+ T cells11,12,13. Yet recent findings have suggested that DC-driven anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity is suppressed in ferroptotic tumours8,9,10,17. Emerging evidence has implicated that the unrestrained generation of membrane lipid peroxides in ferroptotic cells can promote the production and release of molecules that may impact immune cell functions18. However, what causes the suppression of DC-mediated anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity in the context of tumour ferroptosis remains largely unclear.

Potentially relevant immunoregulatory factors produced by ferroptotic cancer cells are oxylipins, bioactive lipids generated through peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane lipids, a hallmark of ferroptosis15. To assess ferroptosis-induced oxylipin production and identify key factors, we profiled the oxylipin secretome of mouse BRAF(V600E) and NRAS(G12D) melanoma, 4T1 breast cancer and MC38 colorectal cancer cells following RSL3-induced ferroptosis. Across all these cancer cell lines, RSL3-treated (ferroptotic) cells displayed increased production of oxylipins compared with untreated (non-ferroptotic) controls (Fig. 1a). Of note, in all groups, the eicosanoid PGE2 was by far the most abundant oxylipin upregulated by ferroptosis induction (Fig. 1a). Similar to ferroptosis induction by RSL3 (which inhibits selenoproteins beyond GPX4), we observed strong PGE2 production after genetic ablation of the ferroptosis-protective enzyme GPX4, ferroptosis induction using the GPX4 inhibitor ML210 or erastin-mediated inactivation of system xc–-mediated cystine import (Extended Data Fig. 1a–f). Thus, ferroptosis may trigger the production of PGE2 in cancer cells, which is a notable finding given the important role of PGE2 for suppression of anticancer immunity19,20,21.

According to recent reports, by contrast, stimulation of ultraviolet B (UVB)-induced apoptosis, doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death or necrocide 1 (NC1)-induced necrotic cell death failed to promote PGE2 production (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1g). However, PGE2 production was induced in cells undergoing necroptosis (Extended Data Fig. 1h). These findings imply that PGE2 production is selectively induced by as yet unknown molecular events in ferroptotic cells and that these events, at least to some extent, may be shared with necroptotic cells.

In a recent development, using liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1), we further validated that ferroptotic cancer cells depend on lipid peroxides to produce PGE2 (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This was not the case for key effectors of other cell death pathways, such as caspases or receptor-interacting serine–threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1; Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). We extended our analyses to a broader panel of mouse and human cancer cells, including established cell lines, cells from spontaneous mouse cancer models and cells from patients with pancreatic cancer. In all these cells, RSL3-induced ferroptosis triggered markedly increased PGE2 production (Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). Together, these data suggest that ferroptosis promotes aberrant production of PGE2 in mouse and human cancer cells, prompting us to investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms and consequences for anticancer immunity.

Sources indicate that effective anticancer immunity often depends on cDC1s22,23, which fulfil essential roles in the priming of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses24,25 and effector differentiation and expansion of CD8+ tumour-infiltrating T lymphocytes (TILs)26,27. These cDC1 functions are impacted by immunoregulatory factors derived from dying cancer cells22,23,28; however, how mediators released by ferroptotic cancer cells impact cDC1s and their functions is not known.

To address this problem, we generated cDC1s from bone marrow cells, exposed them to conditioned medium from RSL3-induced, ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells and assessed their functional properties after activation with polyinosinic–polycytidylic acid (poly(I:C); Fig. 1c). The conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells strongly compromised the capacity of cDC1s to produce CXCL9 (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a), a chemokine required for cDC1-mediated orchestration of CD8+ TIL responses26,29. Similar results were observed for cDC1 production of the T cell stimulatory cytokine interleukin-12 (IL-12)30 (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). By contrast, no impairment was observed for cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from cancer cells undergoing apoptosis or doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Impaired CXCL9 production was similarly observed for splenic cDC1s treated with conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells (Extended Data Fig. 3d). These results suggest that factors released by ferroptotic cancer cells disable cDC1s from producing molecules required to promote anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity.

cDC1 functions are controlled by transcriptional programming31,32. We therefore subjected cDC1s activated by poly(I:C) following exposure to ferroptotic or apoptotic BRAF(V600E) cell conditioned medium to transcriptional profiling by RNA sequencing. We found that ferroptotic, but not apoptotic, cancer cell-derived factors induced prominent transcriptional changes in cDC1s (Fig. 1f), including impaired expression of genes encoding stimulatory cytokines (including Ifnb and Ifnl2), T cell-recruiting chemokines (Cxcl9 and Ccl4) and integrins key for T cell activation (Itgal; Fig. 1f). We also confirmed the inhibitory effect on cDC1 cytokine and chemokine production at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Of note, we did not detect a defect in upregulation of MHC or costimulatory molecules (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 1), implying that ferroptotic cancer cell-derived factors do not prevent cDC1 activation. Of note, many of the genes impaired in cDC1s following exposure to ferroptotic cancer cell-derived factors were shared with a core gene set of PGE2-mediated cDC1 dysfunction (Extended Data Fig. 3f,g and Supplementary Table 1), although genes beyond this set were also impaired. Consistently, gene set enrichment analyses revealed a prominent impairment of PGE2-regulated functional cDC1 genes (Extended Data Fig. 3h), whereas genes associated with migration or antigen processing (that is, molecular programs not regulated by PGE2 signalling in cDC1s19), remained unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 3h). Together, these data suggest that ferroptotic cancer cells promote cDC1 dysfunction and that this is mediated by PGE2.

Similar to cancer cells, ferroptosis induction caused aberrant PGE2 production in Pfa1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a), an established mouse embryonic fibroblast model often used to study the molecular underpinnings of ferroptosis33. This was linked to markedly increased transcript and protein expression of the key PGE2-producing enzyme COX2 (encoded by Ptgs2; Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). Lip-1 treatment rescued this effect (Fig. 2a), whereas stimulation of lipid peroxidation by cumene hydroperoxide promoted both Ptgs2 expression and increased PGE2 production in Pfa1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). Together, these results point towards a requirement of membrane lipid peroxide generation for PGE2 production through transcriptional regulation of COX2. Using COX inhibitors, we also confirmed that COX activity was required for PGE2 production by ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2b), but dispensable for execution of ferroptotic cell death (Fig. 2c).

A key event caused by lipid peroxides in ferroptotic cells is the influx of extracellular Ca2+ (ref. 5), which constitutes an early event in pro-ferroptotic cells before the onset of cell death. Consistently, microscopy imaging revealed high intracellular Ca2+ levels in Pfa1 cells early after RSL3-mediated ferroptosis induction (Fig. 2d,e), which was similarly observed for multiple mouse cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). Time-resolved live cell imaging of ferroptotic Pfa1 cells confirmed that Ca2+ influx followed peroxide accumulation, but occurred before the cell death-associated loss of plasma membrane integrity (Fig. 2f). Of note, preventing Ca2+ influx through polyethylene glycol (PEG)-mediated blockade of membrane permeabilization-enabled osmotic molecule exchange5,34,35 (Fig. 2g and Extended Data Fig. 4i,j) abrogated the upregulation of Ptgs2 mRNA (Fig. 2h) and COX2 protein expression (Fig. 2i) in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells, resulting in a loss of PGE2 production (Fig. 2j). We also validated that lipid peroxide generation was only minimally affected by PEG treatment (Extended Data Fig. 4k,l) and that ferroptotic cells become permeable to other small extracellular molecules5, including sodium ions (Na+; Extended Data Fig. 4m–p).

In a recent development, gain-of-function experiments using ionomycin, which selectively transport extracellular Ca2+ into cells, revealed that Ca2+ influx alone was sufficient to promote COX2 upregulation and PGE2 production across Pfa1, BRAF(V600E) melanoma and MC38 colorectal cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 4q,r). Thus, although small molecules beyond Ca2+ enter ferroptotic cells, they probably do not contribute substantially to the activation of COX-mediated PGE2 production. Consistently, blockade of Ca2+ influx using the Ca2+ chelator EGTA confirmed the relevance of Ca2+ signalling for PGE2 production in ferroptotic cells (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 4s,t).

Industry observers note that ca2+ influx can regulate gene expression via p38 MAPK signalling, which requires p38 MAPK activatory phosphorylation (p-p38). Consistently, ferroptotic Pfa1 cells displayed a prominent increase in p-p38 levels (Fig. 2l,m), which was abolished by PEG treatment (Fig. 2l,m). Moreover, treatment with the selective p38 MAPK inhibitor SB203580 abrogated the upregulation of COX2 expression and PGE2 production in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2n,o), demonstrating the relevance of p38 MAPK signalling for PGE2 production. Of note, the later execution of cell death remained unaffected by p38 MAPK inhibition (Fig. 2p) or blockade of Ca2+ influx (Extended Data Fig. 5a). These results suggest that Ca2+-induced p38 MAPK signalling is not required for ferroptotic cell death. We also confirmed that SB203580 did not induce cell death in non-ferroptotic cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a), and that the death of SB203580-treated ferroptotic Pfa1 cells was rescued by Lip-1 (Fig. 2q).

In a recent development, oxylipin profiling revealed a selective requirement of p38 MAPK signalling for production of PGE2 and other COX-derived eicosanoids in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2r), whereas other oxylipins remained largely unaffected. Similar to Pfa1 cells, PEG-mediated inhibition of Ca2+ influx or inhibition of p38 MAPK abolished PGE2 production in ferroptotic cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 5b–e), demonstrating the relevance of Ca2+-mediated p38 MAPK pathway activation for PGE2 production also in ferroptotic cancer cells. We also confirmed that, in cancer cells, this mechanistic axis is already active in the early phase after ferroptosis induction (Extended Data Fig. 5f–r) and that p38 MAPK signalling is dispensable for the propagation of ferroptotic cell death (Extended Data Fig. 5s–v). Experiments with cells deficient in p38α (the p38 MAPK isoform commonly expressed in cancer cells) further validated that p38 MAPK signalling is required for PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 5w,x), but not their cell death execution (Extended Data Fig. 5y). We conclude that Ca2+-mediated activation of p38 MAPK signalling triggers PGE2 production by ferroptotic cells and that this mechanism is not required for ferroptosis-dependent cancer cell death (Fig. 2s). This molecular uncoupling enables to selectively interfere with p38 MAPK pathway activity to impair PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells while preserving ferroptosis-mediated cancer cell elimination.

To test whether ferroptotic cancer cells depend on PGE2 to promote cDC1 dysfunction, we induced ferroptosis in COX-deficient Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells, which cannot produce PGE2 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–c). We then exposed cDC1s to conditioned medium from ferroptotic Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− or control BRAF(V600E) cells, activated them by poly(I:C) and compared their gene expression profile by RNA sequencing (Fig. 3a). We also included cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from apoptotic BRAF(V600E) cells, to test possible effects of dying cancer cell-derived factors unrelated to ferroptosis. We observed that PGE2 deficiency in ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells prevented cDC1 reprogramming (Fig. 3b) and, consequently, rescued the expression of functional cDC1 genes (for example, Irf8, Ifnl2 and Cxcl9; Fig. 3c). This regain of gene expression was similarly observed in a more detailed analysis of the core functional cDC1 genes selectively suppressed by factors from ferroptotic, but not apoptotic, BRAF(V600E) cells (Fig. 3d).
