The former Plymouth, Bristol Rovers and Wycombe Wanderers forward is in trouble with the law, and this is far from the first time that this has happened.

The former EFL forward Chris Zebroski is back in trouble with the law again. Appearing at Swindon Magistrates' Court on the 7th October, Zebroski pleaded guilty to assault causing actual bodily harm following an incident which was described as an "alcohol-fuelled attack" in which "the 39-year-old headbutted the older man and knocked out one of his teeth, leaving him with a significant purple bruise under his eye.".

Zebroski had been appointed as a player-coach at Southern League side Gosport Borough during the summer.

Chris Zebroski started his career at Swindon Town, but moved to Plymouth Argyle after failing to be offered a senior contract at The County Ground, following a spell with non-league Cirencester City. But he first hit the headlines for all the wrong reasons in August 2007 after he was sacked by the club for gross misconduct following an altercation in the bar during their pre-season tour of Austria the previous month, which left the club captain Paul Wotton with cuts to his head.

Sources indicate that zebroski moved on to Millwall and then to Wycombe Wanderers, but his legal complications continued to pile up. After going on loan to Torquay United, where he was a success in his first season with 19 goals for them in the National League throughout the 2007-08 season, he was given a 12-month community order and a fine for kicking and punching a soldier in a street fight in Torquay in August 2010.

According to recent reports, what are your memories of Chris Zebroski as a player? Let us know in the comments below!

He left Wycombe in 2011 to return to Torquay before moving on to Bristol Rovers, After one unsuccessful season there, he joined Cheltenham Town, but midway through his first season at Whaddon Road he had his contract cancelled after repeatedly pulling out of the first-team squad at short notice.

Sources indicate that his next move was into the non-league game with Eastleigh, but at the end of the 2012-13 season he was picked up by Newport County. Again, he was a success on the pitch, with 12 goals in 35 League Two appearances as the Exiles finished 14th in League Two, but again his extracurricular activities would come to catch up with him.

The law would come to catch up with Zebroski again in the summer of 2015, and this time the matter at hand was far more serious. His second season at Rodney Parade had been less successful than his first, with seven goals scored in 36 appearances, but he found himself back in court in July 2015, pleading guilty to four charges of robbery, attempted robbery and assault in relation to two incidents.

The first of these incidents had come in December 2014, when Zebroski crashed his BMW into a taxi and then attacked a witness - another taxi driver - who filmed him when he got out of the car, trying to take his mobile phone from him.

The BBC reported at the time that: "Zebroski hit Mr Madhu [one of the taxi drivers] in the side of the head and tried to wrestle his mobile phone from him before taking and smashing it. Mr Vladimirej [the other taxi driver] ran off so Zebroski chased him, pushed him to the ground and punched him at least 10 times, saying "give me your phone."" He was also found to have assaulted and attempted to rob two men the following February.

In mitigation, Zebroski's counsel pleaded that his client had an alcohol problem, but neither the court nor his employers were impressed by this explanation. He was sentenced to four years and four months in prison, and had his contract terminated by Newport County.

He was released after serving two years of his prison sentence, and later claimed that he had come close to re-signing for Newport County after leaving prison. At the time, Zebroski stated that, "To get sent to jail had a massive impact, a massive wake-up call," and that, "Playing in jail, it definitely built my character.".

This time there were no further offers from EFL clubs, and Zebroski instead ended up as a non-league journeyman, playing for numerous clubs before arriving at Gosport in the summer as a player/coach, and on the pitch, this hasn't been a bad season for Gosport, who are mid-table in the Southern League Premier Division South.

But it's been a different matter behind the scenes. Manager Simon Lane was sacked just two games into the season, but his replacement, Jermaine McGlashan, left the club for personal reasons on the 7th October, meaning that they're already onto their third manager of the season. Whether it's a coincidence or not that McGlashan left Gosport on the same day that Zebroski pleaded guilty to the latest set of charges brought against him is unknown.

Sources indicate that what is clear about Chris Zebroski's story is that he has been given plenty of chances. After the incidents at Plymouth, Torquay, Cheltenham and Newport, he managed to find someone who would take him on again, but whether this will be the case should he be sentenced to time in prison again is unknown. Zebroski passed forty years of age at the end of October 2026, and his contract position with Gosport will remain unclear until the cost of his latest loss of control is confirmed.

Fans of the clubs for whom he played may well be left wondering what he could have been capable of had he been able to stay on the right side of the law throughout his playing career. And any chances of launching a successful coaching career may already have been blighted by his latest legal problems.

Given that there have been almost two decades since getting sacked by Plymouth and his current predicament during which he might have successfully tackled the underlying issues which lead to these outbreaks of violence, it doesn't seem especially likely that he'll be given many more opportunities within the game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United have spent approximately £95m appointing and dismissing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013, according to BBC Sport, with the total expected to pass £100m following Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival.

United’s latest financial disclosures confirm a fee of £7.584m in connection with appointing Pochettino, who left his role as United States national team head coach earlier this month.

The figure takes the cumulative cost of managerial changes to around £95m, according to BBC Sport’s analysis. That total is expected to rise once the costs of Michael Carrick’s dismissal and appointing Pochettino’s coaching staff are included.

Pochettino signed a two-and-a-half-year contract on 13 November, replacing Carrick after a difficult start to the Premier League season. The club’s Stock Market filing states that the appointment fee will be recognised in its financial accounts for the current quarter. United also confirmed borrowing a further £10m on 16 November, taking the amount drawn on their revolving credit facility to £240m.

Sources indicate that pochettino is United’s ninth full-time managerial appointment since Ferguson’s departure, including Ralf Rangnick’s interim spell. The club have also changed managers during each of the past three seasons.

United’s financial disclosures show that their long-term debt stood at £577.4m on 30 September, while outstanding transfer-fee commitments totalled £417m. Those figures are separate from the cost of appointing and dismissing managers.

A Reuters analysis has put the wider cost of managerial and senior football staff changes above £100m, using a broader calculation. Pochettino now faces the task of improving United’s results, beginning with Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Middlesbrough flew to the top of the Championship with a 2-0 home victory over Bristol City at the weekend, but one key decision made by Kim Hellberg will have got supporters talking.

Middlesbrough have claimed their spot at the summit of the Championship once again after a 2-0 win against Michael Skubala's struggling Bristol City side at The Riverside.

Stoke City's 1-0 win over Birmingham City has allowed Boro to leapfrog Blues, whilst the Potters' inferior goal difference sees Hellberg's side claim top spot for now.

It was a tight win for Boro in the end, who didn't seem wholly convincing, as one substitution made by Hellberg must have had some supporters scratching their heads, as action must be taken in January.

With Boro racing into a 2-0 lead just ten minutes into the second half, the Robins tried to fight their way back into the game and had much the better of chances in the second half.

The away outfit would strike the same post three times, as on another day, Boro may not have gotten so lucky.

With around 15 minutes to go, Hellberg looked to freshen things up and see the game out, as Sam Byram, Will Lankshear, and Luke Ayling replaced Callum Brittain, David Strelec, and Sebastian Berhalter.

Ayling, a natural defender, was put into midfield alongside Aidan Morris, as on-loan Rangers midfielder Connor Barron was left on the bench, and must be wondering exactly what he has to do to get a game.

Barron, 24, joined Middlesbrough on loan from Rangers late in the summer window, and it would be fair to suggest that, at this point, the move has been a waste of time for everyone involved.

The Scottish midfielder has failed to play a single minute of football across any competition since his move to Middlesbrough, including in the Championship, and with the 35-year-old Ayling preferred in midfield over him, his future at the Riverside appears bleak.

Joining the likes of Will Lankshear, Amario Cozier-Duberry, Berhalter, Ashley Phillips, and Radek Vitek to make the move to Teesside in the summer, Barron has largely been forgotten, as surely Boro and Rangers will come to some sort of agreement in January.

According to FootballInsider, back in September, Rangers were considering recalling Barron from his loan spell in England early, and two months on, his situation hasn't improved, and their decision to bring him back to Glasgow has surely only been made easier.

For Boro, Barron won't be a big miss at all, having failed to make any sort of impact during his spell with the club, and, in truth, never really being allowed to do so for one reason or another.

Whether he will return to Ibrox and play any sort of notable role under Derek McInnes remains to be seen, though his situation at Boro will surely alert other clubs across the Championship, who may feel as though he could have an impact with them instead.

What do you make of Barron's situation at Middlesbrough? Does he deserve a chance in the side? Would you be disappointed to see him leave? Share your thoughts below!

With Boro sitting pretty at the top of the table as things stand, head coach Hellberg will have no intention of changing things around anytime soon.

That likely includes bringing Barron into the side, as with Morris, Berhalter, and Pukstas as options in the middle of the park, the Scot was always going to find it difficult to make an impression.

Ayling's introduction over him is surely the final nail in the coffin for his time on Teesside, which will surely end as soon as the winter window opens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

In a recent development, it will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

It has been revealed that russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Recent findings suggest that eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

According to recent reports, toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian remarked. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”.

According to recent reports, still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

Industry observers note that at the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”.

It has been revealed that this was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he said he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

According to recent reports, “It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”.

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”.

No. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9.

Industry observers note that tomorrow’s race will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start on the front row together. It is a reasonable run down to turn one and there are overtaking opportunities through the first few corners at Sepang, with it being similar to the configuration in China, with plenty of lines and moves on offer.

Respect between two great champions 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/fbZ6aoKRyw.

In a recent development, “Very difficult to understand. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”.

On Kimi Antonelli’s track limits breach in Q2:.

“Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”.

In a recent development, lewis Hamilton claims this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). My understanding is the Bahrainis are organising the race this year, while local forces are handling the traffic outside the circuit.

Recent findings suggest that “The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”.

Industry observers note that “I love this energy [from the crowd]. Major, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

“I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”.

Industry observers note that it’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he remarked. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external manufacturer who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”.

Haas have declared that Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave at the end of this season. Ocon now faces an uncertain future, with it difficult to see a spot for him on the F1 grid next season. There are suggestions that the 30-year-old’s replacement will be Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, although nothing has been confirmed on that front. 21-year-old Camara currently leads the Formula 2 championship.

TGR Haas F1 Team and Esteban Ocon will part ways at the conclusion of the 2026 season. With plenty of racing ahead, our focus remains on working together to maximize every opportunity through to the final race of the year.#HaasF1 #F1 pic.twitter.com/4iQAuqnSyA.

It has been revealed that aston Martin have now confirmed their driver line-up for next season, retaining both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. There had been reports that Alonso had been contemplating retirement but the 45-year-old will continue into another season.

Aston Martin Aramco confirms Lance and Fernando will continue as the team's drivers in 2027. Read more: ​https://t.co/ePyjJdyAIB pic.twitter.com/VogFUEbNxy.

Other than the second seat alongside Ollie Bearman at Haas, the only other team to keep an eye on is Racing Bulls, with no definite confirmation on their exact driver line-up for next season.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who mentioned the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:.

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, stated the Scuderia had decided to issue a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

“Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti remarked. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”.

Industry observers note that “It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

“The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”.

Especially with the significant upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

It has been revealed that almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. Here they are and who they were racing for:.

Max Verstappen (Red Bull) Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes) Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes) Esteban Ocon (Force India)Nico Hulkenberg (Renault)Sergio Perez (Force India)Fernando Alonso (McLaren)Lance Stroll (Williams)Carlos Sainz (Toro Rosso)Pierre Gasly (Toro Rosso).

Recent findings suggest that with Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Sources indicate that formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Sources indicate that verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a upcoming floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car update since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

This race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

Reggie Watson Chelsea news continues to build, according to football.london, with the 16-year-old further establishing himself as one of Xabi Alonso’s wildcard options in the first-team squad. Watson has been named in both of Chelsea’s senior squads for their Carabao Cup ties this season.

According to recent reports, he was an unused substitute in the second-round win over Luton Town, then made his full Chelsea debut in the 6-3 win over Leeds United at Stamford Bridge. Watson played the first 45 minutes against Leeds, a reward for his progress since Alonso took charge at Chelsea over the summer.

It has been revealed that every stage of Watson’s rise has come through football.london’s reporting, with Chelsea yet to make any official comment on his long-term role in the squad. The outlet’s football.london report traces how the teenager has moved from pre-season fixtures into genuine first-team contention this term.

Watson played a significant part in Chelsea’s pre-season tour, completing the full 90 minutes of the opening match against Western Sydney Wanderers. He was also part of Chelsea’s travelling squad for the Brentford defeat before the international break. Watson was left out of the matchday squad list for that game, though, as explained in our Brentford line-up report.

Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli was the Chelsea youngster named on the bench for that Brentford trip and came on late in the match, football.london added.

Watson’s form has caught attention away from the first-team picture too. He was one of three Chelsea youngsters nominated for Premier League 2’s Player of the Month award for September, alongside Chizaram Ezenwata and Leo Black, according to football.london.

Black recently signed a two-year contract at Chelsea after impressing on trial, while Watson built his own case by scoring three goals in September. That form explains why the Reggie Watson Chelsea story keeps developing. Alonso keeps pulling him into senior squads instead of leaving him with the academy alone. The head coach has shown similar willingness to adapt his squad elsewhere, as detailed in Alonso’s recent rotation aims.

According to recent reports, chelsea are reported to be facing Portsmouth in a behind-closed-doors friendly this weekend, according to football.london, though the club has not confirmed the fixture publicly. Alonso reportedly wants to keep his squad sharp during an extended three-week international break.

Chelsea’s academy side, known as Cobham Next Gen, have no fixture of their own this weekend. That gap could leave Watson free to train or travel with the first-team squad again, football.london reports.

The teenager will try to impress Chelsea’s first-team staff in that friendly. Nothing is confirmed yet about what his involvement will be once the senior squad returns to action after the international break.

#72515. Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 69m • 📚 Deep Dive (13751 w)

Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 69 min read (13751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~69 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa.
  • Recent findings suggest that across many tropical regions, biodiverse old-growth rainforests have been replaced by tree-cash-crop monocultures, including oil palm, rubber, coffee, cacao and timber plantations5.
  • Industry observers note that the multiple negative effects of land-use change and intensification on tropical biodiversity are increasingly well documented, particularly at the local scale (α-diversity).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity1 in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices2,3,4. Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

Recent findings suggest that across many tropical regions, biodiverse old-growth rainforests have been replaced by tree-cash-crop monocultures, including oil palm, rubber, coffee, cacao and timber plantations5. At the same time, both traditional and modern tropical agroforestry systems6—long regarded as reconciling production with ecological sustainability—are being displaced by more intensive agriculture7,8. Such trends in land-use change and land-use intensification pose a substantial threat to the biodiversity and functioning of tropical ecosystems9,10. Quantifying their effects, however, remains challenging owing to the vast effort required to conduct multitrophic inventories of hyperdiverse tropical ecosystems, the often contrasting responses of different taxa, and the scale-dependence of biodiversity11.

Industry observers note that the multiple negative effects of land-use change and intensification on tropical biodiversity are increasingly well documented, particularly at the local scale (α-diversity). Previous investigations have shown that α-diversity in tropical agricultural systems is typically substantially lower than in forests, with diminished species diversity linked to declines in ecological functions12,13,14,15. Although protected areas are central to mitigating these negative effects16, the long-term persistence of tropical biodiversity will also depend on conservation beyond reserve boundaries. Designing biodiversity-friendly tropical agricultural mosaic landscapes that sustain regional diversity (γ-diversity) without compromising economic objectives is therefore critical3,8,15. Achieving this goal requires a thorough understanding of how community composition varies among sites (β-diversity)17. β-Diversity arises either from species replacement among sites, with each site hosting a different set of species (turnover), or from species-poorer communities forming subsets of species-richer ones (nestedness)18. Identifying the spatial, environmental and management-related drivers of β-diversity in the context of land-use intensification in hyperdiverse tropical ecosystems may thus guide more effective landscape-scale management19.

An important yet understudied process in this context is biotic homogenization, which has been suggested to be the dominant dynamic shaping species communities and global biodiversity in the Anthropocene20. Biotic homogenization occurs when communities become increasingly similar in composition, often through the loss of specialized, rare or forest-dependent species and their replacement by widespread generalists, including non-native species21. By contrast, biotic differentiation occurs when communities become more dissimilar in species composition, arising from local gains, such as the introduction of non-natives, or from species losses, including the extinction of dominant native species17,22. Patterns of species losses and gains can mask the progressive erosion of biota in formerly forested landscapes, thereby obscuring the true magnitude of the global biodiversity crisis. In heterogeneous agricultural landscapes, differentiation can also result from a variety of semi-natural habitats that support distinct species assemblages. Because homogenization and differentiation can occur simultaneously, understanding their combined dynamics is essential for assessing the full impact of land-use intensification—yet this interplay remains insufficiently explored17,22.

Here we fill this knowledge gap through systematic biodiversity inventories of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life, multiple trophic levels, and both aboveground and belowground compartments. Communities were sampled across four different land uses—lowland forests, and three agricultural land uses: low-intensity rubber agroforests (hereafter referred to as jungle rubber) and intensively managed smallholder rubber and oil palm plantations (Fig. 1). Biodiversity and environmental data were collected using a standardized design across 32 sampling plots distributed across 2 distinct landscapes within the smallholder-dominated agricultural tropical lowlands of Jambi Province in Sumatra, Indonesia (Extended Data Fig. 1). This comprehensive dataset builds on a long-term collaborative research programme that has generated detailed taxonomic, functional and trophic information, as well as integrative analyses that link ecological and socio-economic dimensions (Methods). Leveraging this foundation, we provide a novel perspective by investigating the effects of tropical land-use intensification on multitrophic community assemblages at multiple spatial scales. Indonesia combines exceptional biodiversity with one of the world’s highest rates of deforestation, making it a critical frontier of tropical land-use change23,24,25 and a model region for studying land-use trajectories that are increasingly characteristic of smallholder-dominated tropical regions globally.

According to recent reports, a, The studied land-use intensification gradient ranged from lowland forest (F) to three agricultural land uses of increasing intensity: low-intensity jungle rubber agroforest (J), and intensively managed smallholder rubber (R) and oil palm (O) monocultures. b, Our ecosystem-wide assessment included 24 aboveground and belowground taxonomic groups in Sumatra, Indonesia. c, Land-use effects on the number and proportion of species or microbial OTUs. The shading intensity in the Venn diagrams reflects the number and proportion of species, whether considering all taxa together or separating aboveground and belowground taxonomic groups, with darker shading indicating higher values. Icons courtesy of Ira Taliki (a) and Milena Sampaio (b).

We find that the few remaining tropical forests in the region constitute irreplaceable reservoirs of biodiversity. Overall, 5,861 species occurred exclusively in forest (15% of all recorded species in our study; including species, morphospecies and operational taxonomic units (OTUs) or amplicon sequence variants—hereafter referred to as species), including 1,510 aboveground species (30% of all aboveground species) and 4,351 belowground species (12% of all belowground species) (Fig. 1). Forest-dependence was most pronounced for trees, understorey plants and mesostigmatid mites, each with at least 40% of strictly forest-associated species (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3). These estimates are conservative because our sampling design included three times more agricultural plots than forest plots (Supplementary Figs. 1–3), whereas our sampling effort was equal across all four land-use types. Furthermore, the remaining forests in our study landscapes have faced degradation. Thus, the data probably underestimate the biodiversity potential of intact forests and instead reflect the current trajectory of forest degradation26. Together, these results indicate that a significant proportion of the species pool depends on forests, underscoring the urgency of restoring remaining forest habitats while conserving and preventing further agricultural expansion16,27 and ongoing forest degradation28.

It has been revealed that A substantial fraction of biodiversity persisted in agricultural smallholder landscapes: nearly 40% of the recorded species can be considered as forest generalists—that is, species found in both forest and one or more agricultural land uses (15,889 species, 1,966 aboveground and 13,923 belowground taxa). However, almost half of the forest aboveground generalist species (1,966 species) were absent from monocultures and occurred only in forest and jungle rubber (823 species; Fig. 1). At least 60% of aboveground biodiversity (3,057 species) was confined to forest and jungle rubber, and was thus vulnerable to the ongoing loss of (agro)forests13. This trend was especially pronounced for canopy bugs (Hemiptera), hymenopteran parasitoids, spiders and trees (more than 20% of their species were shared only between these two land uses) and bats (40% was shared between these two land uses; Extended Data Fig. 2). Of all belowground species, 19% (6,481 species) were shared across all land uses, with 7% of the species only shared between forest and jungle rubber (2,542 species; Extended Data Fig. 3). The substantial overlap between aboveground forest and jungle rubber communities provides strong empirical evidence that agroforests offer a suitable habitat for a considerably higher number of forest-dependent species than monocultures29,30. Although agroforests cannot replace intact forests, the biodiversity value of traditional agricultural systems, which buffer biodiversity losses in this agricultural landscape, should be recognized. Agroforests also represent a potential leverage point for enhancing biodiversity in human-modified landscapes28, for example, by enriching existing monocultures with native trees3,4.

Overall, land-use intensification drove a marked shift from a species-rich pool of aboveground forest-dependent species to a smaller set of species associated with monocultures. This transition was accompanied by pronounced losses in γ-multidiversity—defined as the average of standardized species richness values across taxonomic groups1 within each land use. Relative to forest (γ-multidiversity = 0.91), γ-multidiversity decreased by 20% in jungle rubber (0.73) and by around 78% in monocultures (0.20) (Fig. 2; Extended Data Fig. 4 for aboveground and belowground γ-multidiversity separately). Thus, our results show clear biodiversity losses with intensification, especially for aboveground species.

a, Significant effects of land use on α-multidiversity (the average of standardized species richness across taxonomic groups at the plot level; R2 = 0.81, F = 38.68, P < 0.001) and β-multidiversity (the average standardized β-diversity across taxonomic groups per plot based on Jaccard, R2 = 0.30, F = 4.06, P = 0.016) using two-sided analysis of variance (ANOVA) type II. Linear model fits using ggeffect (marginal mean and 95% confidence intervals, n = 32 plots). Letters indicate statistically significant pairwise differences (P < 0.05) based on multiple comparisons of means using Tukey’s contrast, with P values adjusted for the false discovery rate. b, Points and lines (mean and 95% confidence intervals using 10,000 bootstrap replicates) represent log ratio in diversity associated with land-use intensification using forests as a control. Confidence intervals not overlapping zero indicate differences from the forest (coloured points; black confidence intervals; paler colours indicate when the 95% confidence intervals include zero). Negative and positive values indicate decreases (loss of species richness or homogenization) or gains in species richness and differentiation when compared to mean forest values, respectively. For β-multidiversity components, negative and positive values similarly represent decreases or increases in turnover or nestedness relative to forest turnover and nestedness; values for single taxonomic groups are shown in Extended Data Fig. 6.

We hypothesized that land-use intensification would consistently reduce α-diversity across taxa and promote biotic homogenization, such that an agricultural land-use type would harbour more similar communities (lower β-diversity) than forests. By contrast, biotic differentiation occurs when communities become more dissimilar in species composition under an agricultural land use than in forests. To test this hypothesis, we quantified α-diversity as local species richness and α-multidiversity. The α-multidiversity is defined as the average of standardized species richness across taxonomic groups at the plot level1 for each land use using the min–max scaling approach (Methods). To assess changes in community composition within each land use, we quantified β-diversity as aggregated pairwise dissimilarities per plot, and β-multidiversity as the average standardized β-diversity across taxonomic groups per plot using the min–max scaling approach.

Sources indicate that we observed a substantial decline in α-multidiversity with land-use intensification (R2 = 0.81, F = 38.68; P < 0.001; Fig. 2, Extended Data Table 1 and Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5), decreasing from 0.59 in forest (95% confidence interval: 0.54–0.65) to 0.47 in jungle rubber (95% confidence interval: 0.42–0.52) and 0.26 and 0.28 in rubber and oil palm plantations, respectively (95% confidence intervals: 0.21–0.32 and 0.23–0.34, respectively; Fig. 2 and Extended Data Table 1). This corresponds to an approximately 50% loss of α-multidiversity from forest to monocultures (Fig. 2). Significant declines relative to forest were observed in 15, 21 and 21 taxonomic groups in jungle rubber, rubber and oil palm plantations, respectively, corresponding to 75%, 94%, and 100% of aboveground taxa, and 38%, 75%, and 63% of belowground taxa (Fig. 2). Trees exhibited the strongest shifts, as they are directly affected by deforestation, planting, and current management practices (herbicide application, manual weeding, liming and fertilizer use), as well as by altered microclimatic and soil-related site conditions in plantations13,30. Such biodiversity losses in monocultures may be partly mitigated locally by improved management31 and diversified, sustainable production systems3,4.

According to recent reports, soil bacteria across agricultural land uses and archaea in oil palm plantations were the only groups in which significant species gains relative to forests were observed (Fig. 2). Species gains for these groups can emerge, for example, as a result of management practices such as liming and fertilization, which increase the soil pH32 and the availability of bio-available nitrogen improving growth conditions for specific bacterial and archaeal taxa33. However, these groups show pronounced shifts in community composition and biotic homogenization (details below; Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 4), highlighting that changes in species richness alone cannot capture the ecosystem-wide effects of land-use intensification.

According to recent reports, β-Multidiversity showed only subtle, yet significant, changes across land uses (based on standardized Jaccard; R2 = 0.30, F = 4.06, P = 0.016; Fig. 2 and Extended Data Table 2). This less pronounced multidiversity loss was partly explained by taxon-specific patterns of biotic homogenization or differentiation (Fig. 2). Significant biotic homogenization—lower β-diversity in the agricultural land uses relative to β-diversity in forests—was found in 5, 6 and 9 taxonomic groups in jungle rubber, rubber and oil palm, respectively; whereas 9, 13 and 12 groups showed significant differentiation—higher β-diversity in the agricultural land uses relative to forests. The remaining groups showed neither significant homogenization nor differentiation. Only 10 out of 24 taxonomic groups responded consistently across agricultural systems—either homogenization (understorey plants, fungi and bacteria) or differentiation (canopy bugs, flies, parasitoids, spiders, butterflies, leaf litter beetles and oribatid mites; Fig. 2).

Recent findings suggest that idiosyncratic responses probably reflect land-use-specific effects on habitats and the interactions between disturbance and environmental heterogeneity19,34 (Supplementary Fig. 5). For example, biotic and abiotic filtering may drive homogenization in tree communities by directly causing the loss of forest specialists through management. Effects can also act indirectly via resource homogenization—for example, through fertilization or homogenization of plant resources in terms of composition and seasonality, impacting niche segregation across trophic and non-trophic interactions. Further indirect effects act via seed dispersal, recruitment, growth and survival34. Similarly, homogenization in soil microbial communities may arise from filtering through shifts in plant–fungal associations35 and from reduced dispersal limitation via passive dispersal36,37,38. By contrast, biotic differentiation can arise from spillover and occasional species, as observed previously in arthropods19 and supported by our results on abundance-based dissimilarity indices for canopy arthropods (Supplementary Results). Biotic homogenization and differentiation can result not only from changes in community composition but also from changes in spatial aggregation, species abundance distributions and individual densities per unit area39. These ecological mechanisms are biologically relevant, modified by land-use intensification and captured by our approach39.

Turnover was the dominant component of β-multidiversity across land uses, ranging from zero in oil palm for trees to 0.93 in rubber for leaf litter spiders. Turnover multidiversity reflects the extent to which sites within the same land use host distinct species assemblages across multiple taxonomic groups. Turnover multidiversity increased in jungle rubber (log ratio: 0.07; 95% confidence interval: 0.02 to 0.11) and decreased in monocultures (log ratio rubber: −0.10; 95% confidence interval: −0.15 to −0.06 and log ratio oil palm: −0.09; 95% confidence interval: −0.13 to −0.05) compared with forest (Fig. 2). Stronger declines in turnover multidiversity were observed in oil palm for aboveground taxa (log ratio: −0.10; 95% confidence interval: −0.15 to −0.07) and in rubber for belowground taxa (log ratio: −0.30; 95% confidence interval: −0.44 to −0.22; Extended Data Fig. 6). Nestedness across land uses ranged from 0.02 in jungle rubber for fungi to 0.48 in rubber for centipedes. Relative to forest, nestedness multidiversity—indicating assemblages in species-poor sites forming subsets of those in species-rich sites within the same land use across taxonomic groups—increased for aboveground taxa in rubber (log ratio: 0.38; 95% confidence interval: 0.27–0.47) and oil palm (log ratio: 0.32; 95% confidence interval: 0.23–0.44) plantations and decreased on belowground taxa in jungle rubber (log ratio: −0.44; 95% confidence interval: −0.58 to −0.28) and oil palm (log ratio: −0.40; 95% confidence interval: −0.52 to −0.18) plantations (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 6).

Recent findings suggest that our results reveal that disentangling the components underlying biotic differentiation within each land use is essential; differentiation emerging from nested assemblages has different implications for conservation and landscape management than differentiation emerging from the uniqueness of species assemblages. Distinguishing these processes sharpens our ability to anticipate trajectories of biotic homogenization, including the delayed effects of extinction debt and colonization lags, whereby an apparent differentiation may in fact reflect assemblage simplification before a transition towards homogenization occurs17,19,22. Biotic differentiation can emerge when differences—for example, in local landscape properties—among sites lead to increasing differentiation over time, resulting in homogenization within the same landscape but differentiation among landscapes (landscape divergence hypothesis)40. Weak homogenization or biotic differentiation can also result from higher forest cover in smallholder landscapes; forest cover may guard against homogenization through, for example, edge effects and source-sink dynamics. Smallholder plantations in our study region lie at the deforestation frontier41—other regions that have undergone earlier land-use change may consist of larger, more homogenous, intensively managed industrial plantations (not included in our study). Therefore, higher levels of homogenization and shifts from differentiation to homogenization are expected as smallholders allocate more land to the main crop42 and optimize management and logistics to increase crop profitability8,41,43 and on large-scale industrial plantations. These considerations help to identify points of intervention in existing plantations and in plantations that are entering second and third generations to increase differentiation and promote more sustainable landscapes2,3,4.

In a recent development, land uses differed markedly in species composition, as shown by the ordination of mean pairwise community dissimilarities aggregated across all taxonomic groups (Fig. 3) and the analyses of similarities (ANOSIM; R = 0.92; P < 0.001). Compositional shifts from forests to monocultures were primarily associated with changes in microclimate and vegetation structure (Fig. 3). These results were corroborated by a multiple factor analysis, which identifies a common structure across two or more data matrices without assuming causal relationships44. The common structure across taxonomic groups and environmental variables aligned with land use (the first dimension explains 18% of the variance and was associated with land-use type), and was mostly driven by compositional shifts in fungi, protists, bacteria, oribatid mites, and canopy spiders and bugs (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 6). A previous study, using the same plots, demonstrates a compositional shift in terms of a loss of plant symbionts and a gain of pathogenic fungi with land-use intensification35, despite almost no change in fungal richness across land uses. Therefore, understanding compositional shifts in soil communities is highly relevant because they affect ecosystem functioning—for example, via aboveground–belowground interactions and nutrient cycling33,35.
