Polygons delineate land-use types. Vectors indicate environmental variables, grouped by category. The categories are microclimate (blue: air temperature, mean air temperature; rel. humidity, mean relative air humidity (%); soil moisture, mean soil moisture (vol%); soil temperature, mean soil temperature); vegetation (light green: canopy openness; fine roots, fine root productivity; mean ENL, mean effective number of vegetation layers; mean SSC, mean stand structural complexity; s.d. ENL, standard deviation effective number of vegetation layers; and s.d. SSC, standard deviation stand structural complexity); litter (pink: litter C, litter carbon content; litterfall; and litter N, litter nitrogen content); and soil properties (brown: bulk density; ECEC, effective cation exchange capacity; base saturation; extractable P, Bray extractable phosphorus; pH, soil pH; soil 15N, soil 15N natural abundance signature; soil Al, aluminium saturation; soil C:N, soil C:N ratio; soil organic C, soil organic carbon; soil respiration; and soil total N, soil total nitrogen).

According to recent reports, identifying primary drivers of biodiversity change is crucial to landscape management. Studies of β-diversity have often contrasted the roles of ecologically neutral processes with those of niche-based community assembly45,46,47. Strong contributions of geographical distance to β-diversity indicate a prevalence of neutral, dispersal-related processes, whereas strong contributions of environmental variables indicate an vital role of habitat filtering48. To disentangle the relative contributions of geographical distance, environmental differences and landscape context to β-diversity, we performed generalized dissimilarity modelling (GDM)49. The GDMs explained substantial variation in β-diversity (>50%) for understorey plants, fungi, bacteria, protists, canopy spiders, beetles, bugs, parasitoids and springtails, as well as trees, archaea, butterflies and oribatid mites (Fig. 4). The variation in pairwise β-diversity was strongly related to environmental variables, particularly vegetation and litter availability, both of which vary with land-use types42. By contrast, geographic distance contributed only weakly to β-diversity for most taxonomic groups (Fig. 4). This suggests a stronger role of habitat filtering, rather than dispersal, in structuring the species assemblages in the landscape mosaic under study.

Results from GDM. For each group of environmental variables, principal components were calculated and selected until the cumulative explained variance reached 80%; these components were used as predictors in the GDM. Colour shading denotes individual principal component dimensions. Variable loadings are shown in Extended Data Fig. 7. Model statistics and predictor importance using Monte Carlo sampling with 250 permutations are reported in Supplementary Tables 2 and 3. Landscape context is represented by the mean forest cover within a 200 m concentric buffer surrounding each plot.

Sources indicate that the three taxonomic groups with the strongest explanatory power—understorey plants, fungi and bacteria—also exhibited homogenization in the agricultural land uses (Fig. 2). This pattern suggests that homogenization is driven, to a large extent, by deterministic processes associated with land-use-induced changes in the environment, including direct impacts from soil disturbance and fertilization, and indirect effects from the deliberate replacement of forest species with a single, often non-native, target crop, and an alteration of vegetation structure by establishing even-aged structure. Additionally, biotic homogenization is driven by characteristics of the surrounding landscape (Supplementary Table 3). Processes leading to biotic differentiation can also emerge from changes in vegetation structure, as observed in most canopy-dwelling groups. Thus, for many groups, homogenization and differentiation can be linked to drastic changes in habitat structure following land-use intensification30 and in the remaining surrounding forests. Still, biotic differentiation can also be only weakly related to environmental conditions and the surrounding landscape, as for leaf litter spiders, mesostigmatid mites and springtails. Thus, biotic differentiation could be more stochastic and potentially driven by disturbance, legacy effects or meta-population and meta-community dynamics that were not quantified here.

According to recent reports, our results provide detailed insights into how tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity through concurrent changes in species richness and community composition. We document pronounced declines in γ- and α-multidiversity from lowland forests to monocultures, driven primarily by aboveground taxa. The diminishing tropical (degraded) forests and traditional agroforestry systems in our study region constitute irreplaceable reservoirs of biodiversity, but their biodiversity is in peril and requires urgent conservation and restoration actions. Divergent responses between aboveground and belowground compartments underscore the need to integrate multiple taxonomic groups spanning body size and mobility. We found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, consistent with previous work, we found taxon-specific and seemingly idiosyncratic patterns of both biotic homogenization and differentiation19,20,22,50, but we also revealed a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness in monocultures. Our results call for careful interpretation of spatial patterns of community homogenization and differentiation, as well as long-term monitoring, because homogenization–differentiation trends can be scale-dependent (in line with the landscape divergence hypothesis) and can differ between smallholder and industrial plantations, which are not included in our study. In addition, early stages of assemblage simplification may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization. Overall, our results demonstrate that land-use intensification alters multidiversity across spatial scales, with ecosystem-wide consequences for biotic communities and their abiotic environment, and suggest that habitat filtering has a stronger role than neutral or dispersal processes. Effective conservation will benefit from recognizing the conservation value of traditional agricultural systems, which, in our study region, buffer the loss of multiple generalist forest species and exhibit high levels of β-diversity. These traditional agricultural systems are at the moment under pressure from conversion and lie outside the conservation focus and landscape planning. Furthermore, implementing sustainable management practices2,3,4 within conventional monocultures could help mitigate biodiversity losses and promote landscape differentiation in these agricultural landscapes. Differentiation across multiple taxonomic groups should not overshadow the homogenization occurring within key taxonomic groups such as bats, birds, trees and understorey plants. Therefore, there is a growing need to establish conservation priorities for focal taxonomic groups, including tailored landscape-scale solutions to maximize the γ-diversity of forest-associated biodiversity, such as conserving irreplaceable endemic species in this biodiversity hotspot.

Recent findings suggest that our study was conducted in the province of Jambi on the island of Sumatra, Indonesia. This tropical lowland region has undergone extensive land-use changes since the twentieth century and is a showcase of smallholder agriculture in Indonesia13,42. Two sample landscapes, ‘Harapan’ and ‘Bukit Duabelas’ (with loam and clay Acrisol soils, respectively), were selected within Jambi Province. In each landscape, four 50 m × 50 m replicate plots were established in each of the four land-use types common to the region: primary degraded forest (sensu ref. 51), jungle rubber (a traditional agroforestry system established by planting rubber trees inside secondary forest), smallholder monoculture rubber plantation, and smallholder monoculture oil palm plantation—totalling 32 plots. The number of replicate sites per land use is comparable to that of other ecological studies in tropical lowland regions52. Various measurements, such as microclimate, were taken at the plot level. Other measurements, such as most biodiversity sampling, were taken in five permanent 5 m × 5 m subplots established within each plot. All sites were selected in 2012. At this time, rubber plantations were established 7–16 years ago, and oil palm plantations were established 8–15 years ago. For jungle rubber, plots selected contained older non-rubber trees, with individual rubber trees of varying ages not planted in rows13.

Industry observers note that jungle rubber, rubber and oil palm plots were owned and managed by smallholder farmers, whereas the forest plots were located in the Bukit Duabelas National Park and the Harapan Rainforest Restoration concession area (PT REKI). In our study region, smallholders generally do not cultivate food crops alongside the target cash crops examined here, with only a few exceptions8,42,43. Our study’s oil palm plots were on average surrounded by ~13.6% forest and ~61% oil palm plantations within 1 km buffers compared with ~0.45% and ~96% in industrial oil palm plantations, respectively41. Further, our oil palm plots received less herbicide (0.73 l ha−1 year−1) and fertilizer (6.6 kg N ha−1 year−1) compared with industrial oil palm plantations41 (1.12 l ha−1 year−1 and 141 kg N ha−1 year−1). Rubber and oil palm smallholder plantations represent the highest land-use intensity level among the systems included in our study. Yet land-use intensity is even higher in large-scale industrial plantations. More information on the study region, study design, land-use types and management practices of the smallholder systems is provided elsewhere8,13,42. Data compilation in these studies has also served as a basis for our study, but has been substantially expanded in recent years. For example, a multi-taxon perspective was offered in ref. 42 for 3 taxonomic groups, in ref. 13 for 9 taxonomic groups, and in ref. 8 for 14 taxonomic groups.

Recent findings suggest that we studied 24 different biodiversity indicators distributed from the canopy to the soil, namely: (1) ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae), (2) beetles (Coleoptera), (3) true bugs (Hemiptera), (4) flies (Diptera)53, (5) parasitoids (parasitoid Hymenoptera), (6) spiders (Araneae), and (7) springtails (Collembola), from the canopy; (8) bats (Chiroptera), (9) birds (Aves), (10) butterflies (Lepidoptera), (11) trees (Tracheophyta), (12) understorey plants (Tracheophyta), (13) spiders, (14) beetles, and (15) ants, from the leaf litter; (16) centipedes (Chilopoda), (17) springtails, (18) mesostigmatid mites (Mesostigmata), and (19) oribatid mites (Oribatida), from the litter and soil; and (20) fungi, (21) testate amoebae, (22) protists, (23) bacteria, and (24) archaea, from the soil (Supplementary Table 4). These biodiversity indicators represent a wide spectrum of taxa, encompassing all domains of life, various trophic levels, and diverse ecological strategies, dispersal abilities and body sizes. This comprehensive dataset builds on a long-term collaborative effort that generated detailed insights into individual taxonomic groups, including species descriptions54,55,56,57,58,59, field guides60,61,62,63 and functional and trophic interactions53,64,65,66—as well as ecosystem-wide analyses and integrative studies linking ecological and socio-economic dimensions8,13,42.

Industry observers note that canopy arthropods (ants, beetles, bugs, flies, parasitoids, spiders and springtails) were collected by canopy fogging in the dry season from May to October 2013. In each of the 32 plots, 3 representative canopy locations were selected, avoiding canopy gaps and overly dense canopies. At each of the 3 locations, 16 rectangular traps (1 m × 1 m) fitted with 100 ml ethanol-filled bottles were suspended from ropes beneath the selected canopies at approximately 1.50 m. 50 ml of DECIS EC 25 (active ingredient: deltamethrine 25 g l−1), dissolved in 4 l of petroleum white oil, was applied to the target canopies from the ground using the Swingtec Swingfog SN 50. In all four land-use systems, target canopies consisted of leaves from different trees. Stunned and dead arthropods were collected from the traps up to 2 h after the complete application of the fogging mixture. Canopy fogging was conducted in the early morning, immediately after sunrise, to minimize air movement that would disperse the fog. This was done only in dry conditions, ensuring that small arthropods would not become trapped in water droplets on leaves and branches. Overall, 372,146 canopy arthropod individuals were collected this way53 and sorted into morphospecies for selected taxa. This study includes data from the following taxa: ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) 179 morphospecies67; beetles (Coleoptera) 397 morphospecies in 4 families (Chrysomelidae, Curculionidae, Elateridae and Staphylinidae)68; true bugs (Hemiptera) 301 morphospecies in 2 suborders (Auchenorrhyncha and Heteroptera); flies (Diptera) 483 morphospecies in 2 suborders (Brachycera and Nematocera, including Eudiptera)69; parasitoid wasps (Hymenoptera: “Parasitica”) 1,012 morphospecies in 6 families (Braconidae, Ceraphronidae, Encyrtidae, Eulophidae, Scelionidae and Platygastridae)70; spiders (Araneae) 445 morphospecies71; and springtails (Collembola) 60 morphospecies72. Recorded (morpho-)species across taxa are deposited in the http://ecotaxonomy.org database and in refs. 60,61,62.

According to recent reports, bats were surveyed using mist nets and harp traps between April and August 2015. We used telescopic aluminium poles to install mist nets with a total length of 48 m, as well as two harp traps (1.35 m × 1.75 m) in presumed bat flyways. Mist nets were 3 m high, with a 19-mm mesh size, and were installed at ground level or up to 3 m high, depending on plot conditions. Each plot was sampled from 17:30 to 22:00 on two consecutive nights, resulting in an average sampling effort of 1,296 m2 of mist net hours. We checked the nets and traps every 15 min until 20:00 and every 30 min thereafter. Harp traps were left on site until and checked the morning after. Captured bats were left in tissue pouches until the nets were closed. Then bat morphology was measured to identify them according to the latest bat species checklist for Sumatra73. We tagged the bats’ nails with nail polish colour codes to identify recaptures and released them afterwards. This study includes data from 20 bat species. In plot HJ3, no individuals were caught (total abundance = 0).

According to recent reports, birds were sampled with point counts74, as well as automated sound recordings, from May to July 2013. Point counts and automated sound recordings lasted 20 min and were conducted from the centre of each plot between 6:00 and 10:00. The timing of point counts alternated between early and late morning, and all plots were visited three times. The automated sound recorders (SM2+ with two SMX-II microphones, Wildlife Acoustics) were set up at ~2 m height to record at a 44.1 kHz sampling rate in stereo, simultaneously across land-use types; one recording, starting at sunrise, was used for each plot. Point count detections of individuals flying above the canopy were excluded, and unfamiliar bird calls were recorded using a Sennheiser ME-66 directional microphone. The automated sound recordings were uploaded to ecoSound-web, an online platform for ecoacoustics75, for two independent ornithologists to identify all bird calls within an estimated 35 m radius. Only bird species identified by both ornithologists in recordings of each plot were used and subsequently merged with the species list obtained from the point counts. Aural detections were confirmed with cross-checks on the Xeno-Canto online bird call database (https://xeno-canto.org/). This study encompasses data from 114 bird species. For birds, BO1_5 data were unavailable. Therefore, when analyses required non-missing values, imputation was performed by using the average from plots of the same land use within the same landscape (that is, Bukit). However, γ-diversity values for birds may be underestimated.

Butterflies (Lepidoptera: Papilionidae, Pieridae, Lycaneidae and Nymphalidae) were recorded from all 32 study plots in the dry season of 2017 between August and October. Butterflies were collected using sweep netting on three parallel 50-m transects per plot, with two transects on the outer boundaries and the third through the centre. Sweep netting was conducted once in the morning (8:00−11:00) and repeated in the afternoon (13:00−16:00). Except for two voucher specimens per collected species, all butterfly individuals were released on the evening of the sampling day. This study includes data based on butterfly specimens from 219 species76. Recorded morphospecies are deposited in the http://ecotaxonomy.org database and in ref. 63.

Plant inventories were conducted between February 2013 and August 2014, using different sampling schemes for large trees and vascular understorey plants30. All trees per plot with a diameter of ≥10 cm at a height of 1.3 m were identified. Vascular understorey plants were censused in the five 5 m × 5 m subplots per plot, including all plant individuals, such as terrestrial plants (herbs, shrubs, climbers and juvenile trees) and epiphytes growing up to 3 m above the ground. 281 tree species were present in both censuses (for large trees and understorey plants). To avoid inflating species richness, they were retained only in the matrix that included large trees. Species identification was conducted in the field if possible or otherwise based on field photographs and herbarium specimens deposited at BIOT, BO, GOET, and the herbaria at Jambi University and Harapan Rainforest (acronyms follow Index Herbarium: http://sweetgum.nybg.org/science/ih/). The number of all individuals per species and plot was used for analyses. In total, this study includes 443 tree species and 976 vascular plant species in the understorey.

According to recent reports, leaf litter was collected from three of the five subplots within each of the study plots. In each subplot, leaf litter from 1 m2 of ground was sieved using a coarse mesh (width of 2 cm). All macro-invertebrates visible to the naked eye were hand-collected from the sieved samples, stored in 65% ethanol and transported to the laboratory for identification12. Recorded (morpho-)species are deposited in the http://ecotaxonomy.org database. This study includes data on 135 morphospecies of ants, 170 morphospecies of beetles, and spider specimens from 132 morphospecies. For leaf litter spiders and leaf litter beetles, no individuals were detected in plots HO2 and BO4, respectively (total abundance = 0).

According to recent reports, between October and November 2013, random samples were taken from three 5 m × 5 m subplots per plot (a total of 96 samples). Samples were taken at least 2 m from the next tree or dead-wood accumulation. Each sample measured 16 cm × 16 cm and included the complete litter layer and the underlying topsoil to a depth of 5 cm, obtained using a spade. Animals were extracted using heat and stored in 70% ethanol77. This study includes data from 12 morphospecies. In plot BR2, no individuals were detected (total abundance = 0).

Samples were taken in October 2013. In each plot, one randomly positioned soil core (16 cm × 16 cm) was taken to a depth of 5 cm in the mineral soil. Litter and soil layers were separated in the field and extracted independently. Animals were extracted by heat for 5–10 days until the substrate was completely dry78, collected in dimethyleneglycol–water solution (1:1) and stored in 70% ethanol79. This study includes data from 58 morphospecies.

Recent findings suggest that three soil cores were taken in October and November 2013 from each of 32 plots. Soil cores (16 cm × 16 cm) were collected from the litter layer and the underlying soil to a depth of 5 cm. Animals were extracted under a heat gradient78, collected in dimethyleneglycol–water solution (1:1) and thereafter stored in 70% ethanol. Identification of soil mites was done on microscopic slides to (morpho)species level. Recorded (morpho)species are deposited in the http://ecotaxonomy.org database. More details are described in ref. 80. This study includes data from 110 morphospecies of mesostigmatid mites and 219 morphospecies of oribatid mites.

Soil samples were collected in October and November 2016. In three subplots (5 m × 5 m) per plot, five soil cores (15 cm depth, 4 cm diameter) were taken and pooled, yielding a total of three samples per plot. Samples were sieved (50 × 50 mm mesh) and freeze-dried. DNA extraction, sequencing, and assignment of OTUs have been described81. Data have been deposited in the Dryad repository82. This study includes data from 12,309 OTUs.

Sources indicate that litter and upper mineral soil samples (to a depth of 50 mm) were collected in October and November 2013 using a 50 mm diameter corer. Testate amoebae were extracted from the samples by washing 1 g dry weight sample through a 500-µm mesh and back-sieving the filtrate through a 10-µm mesh. More details are described in ref. 83. This study includes data from 190 morphospecies of testate amoebae.

According to recent reports, soil samples were collected from each study plot and processed (sieving, freeze-drying and milling) to extract DNA for protist community analysis84. This study includes data from 5,204 OTUs of protists.

Soil samples were taken at the subplot level, DNA was extracted and amplicons were generated with primer pairs targeting the 16S ribosomal RNA gene of bacteria and archaea and used to assess bacterial and archaeal community compositions separately33. This study includes data on 16,413 bacterial OTUs and 448 archaeal amplicon sequence variants. For archaea, HF3 data were unavailable. Therefore, when analyses required non-missing values, imputation was performed by using the average from plots with the same land use within the same landscape (that is, Harapan). However, γ-diversity values for archaea may be underestimated.

We consider 24 environmental variables distributed into 4 groups: microclimate, vegetation, litter and soil (Supplementary Table 5).

Industry observers note that meteorological stations were set up in the centre of each plot to measure hourly below-canopy air temperature and relative humidity at 2 m height between June 2013 and October 2014. Additionally, soil sensors were used to measure soil temperature and moisture at a depth of 0.3 m (ref. 85).

Recent findings suggest that different aspects of structural complexity have been measured using terrestrial laser scanning in each of the 32 plots in September and October 2016. Based on a single-scan approach, we calculated the effective number of layers, which quantifies vertical stratification86, and the stand structural complexity index87, which describes the complexity of vegetation’s three-dimensional occupation of space. We collected nine single scans, evenly distributed across each plot, and aggregated at the plot level using mean and standard deviation, the latter describing the spatial heterogeneity of vegetation structure88. Additionally, hemispherical photographs were taken at 1.2 m above the ground from 32 positions within each plot to derive canopy openness42. Fine root production was estimated by installing 16 ingrowth cores per plot8.

Aboveground litterfall was assessed by placing 16 litter traps (75 cm × 75 cm) in each plot. Traps were emptied monthly from March 2013 to April 2014. For oil palms, pruned leaves were counted, and a subsample was dried and weighed. For litter nutrients, aliquots of material from the litter–fermentation layer of all 32 plots were dried at 65 °C for 72 h, milled, and analysed for total C and N concentrations using an elemental analyser89 (Carlo Erba Instruments).

Sources indicate that soil sampling was conducted in 2013. Within a 50 m × 50 m area at each site, ten grid points were selected (including the five subplots), and soil samples were taken from the top 0–0.1 m depth. The ten subplots were averaged to represent each site. Soil biochemical characteristics (that is, pH, soil organic carbon (kg C m−2), total nitrogen (g N m−2), 15N natural abundance signatures (‰ 15N), effective cation exchange capacity (ECEC; mmolc m−2), base saturation (%), aluminium saturation (%) and extractable phosphorus (g P m−2)) were determined on air-dried and sieved (2 mm) soil samples. Organic carbon and total nitrogen were analysed using a CN analyser (Vario EL Cube, Elementar Analysis Systems) and 15N by isotope ratio mass spectrometry (Delta Plus, Finnigan MAT). ECEC was determined by percolating the soils with unbuffered 1 mol l−1 NH4Cl, and cations (Ca, Mg, K, Na, Al, Fe and Mn) were measured in percolates using an inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometer (iCAP 6300 Duo VIEW ICP Spectrometer, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Base and aluminium saturation were calculated as percentage exchangeable bases or aluminium on the ECEC. Extractable phosphorus was determined using the Bray 2 method for acidic tropical soils. Soil physical characteristics for each site included bulk density (g cm−3; core method)32,90. Soil respiration was measured monthly in 2013 using a chamber located on four subplots per plot. Gas samples were analysed using a gas chromatograph with an electron capture detector and a flame ionization detector (GC 6000 Vega Series2, Carlo Erba Instruments)91.

Sources indicate that species matrices. Species observations taken at the subplot level were aggregated into plot-level observations.

Environmental data. We conducted a principal component analysis for each group of variables, with variables transformed (when needed) and scaled. We selected the first components until the cumulative explained variance reached 80%. Variable contributions of these selected principal components are displayed in Extended Data Fig. 7.

It has been revealed that landscape data. We calculated landscape metrics within 200 m buffers around our plot centres using a manually classified land-use map derived from satellite imagery from 2016 (ref. 92). We used the R package landscapemetrics93 to calculate the mean forest coverage.

Species occurrences were calculated separately for each taxonomic group.

Recent findings suggest that α- and γ-diversities. We quantified diversity using the Hill number framework, expressing it as effective species numbers, where q0 disregards species abundances and is therefore more sensitive to rare species (species richness) and q1 weights species in proportion to their abundances, favouring neither rare nor dominant species (that is, effective number of common species; Shannon diversity)94. In addition, we calculated rarefaction–extrapolation curves for the 24 taxonomy groups at plot (that is, α-diversity; Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2) and each land use (that is, γ-diversity; Supplementary Fig. 3) level using the iNEXT R package95,96.

α- and γ-multidiversity. To assess the multidiversity across all 24 taxonomic groups, first, we normalized the observed effective number of species at the plot or land-use type level using the min–max scaling approach, following: y = (x − min(x))/(max(x) − min(x)), where x is the set of observed effective number of species. The normalized effective number of species (y) ranges between 0 and 1, with 0 referring to the lowest observed value and 1 to the highest observed value for each taxonomic group across plots or land uses. This method ensures equal weight for all taxonomic groups, despite differences in their diversity ranges, and is a common approach in multi-taxon studies1,97. To obtain a single α-diversity index, we averaged the normalized values—that is, the overall diversity across all taxonomic groups at the plot level (α-multidiversity). For γ-multidiversity, we likewise averaged the normalized values—that is, based on the lowest and highest observed diversity values at the land-use types. In addition, we calculated α- and γ-multidiversity separately for aboveground and belowground taxonomy groups.

β-Diversity and β-multidiversity. For each taxonomic group, we calculated β-diversity using pairwise dissimilarity matrices (presence–absence data; index family = jaccard; Supplementary Fig. 7). The Jaccard pairwise dissimilarity (βjacc, total β-diversity) among plots was computed as βjacc = βjtu + βjne, where βjtu accounted for turnover and βjne accounted for the nestedness (measured as the nestedness-resultant dissimilarity fraction of Jaccard dissimilarity), measured on a normalized scale from 0 to 1. Calculations were performed using the beta.pair from the package betapart v1.6. Mathematically, in cases of complete biodiversity loss—that is, zero individuals detected—plots have a total β-diversity of one as they do not share species with other plots; in these cases, we assumed turnover to be 0 and nestedness to be 1, considering that β-diversity result from species losses; this was implemented manually as it is not included in the output of betapart98,99. We also calculated β-diversity using Sørensen and its components and the abundance-based indices Bray–Curtis (weights absolute differences in abundance equally, so that abundant species contribute most to dissimilatiry)100 and Morisita–Horn (weighted towards common and dominant species and it is robust to sample size)101. These abundance-based dissimilarity indices were calculated using the vegan R package102 (Bray–Curtis: method = “bray”, binary = F; and Morisita–Horn dissimilarity: method = “horn”, binary = F; Supplementary Fig. 8). For Morisita–Horn, it is not possible to calculate dissimilarity when communities have zero abundance. Therefore, for Morisita–Horn, plots with at least one taxon for which the abundance was zero were excluded (BO4, BR2, HJ3, HO2 and HR4). We aggregated the pairwise dissimilarities to a mean pairwise dissimilarity for each taxonomic group for each plot (n = 32 plots for 24 taxonomic groups). To calculate β-multidiversity, we normalized the aggregated pairwise dissimilarity at the plot level using the min–max scaling approach1,97, as y = (x − min(x))/(max(x) − min(x)), where x is the set of pairwise dissimilarity at plot level. The normalized pairwise dissimilarity (y) ranges between 0 and 1, with 0 referring to the lowest observed value and 1 to the highest observed value for each taxonomic group across plots. We average the normalized β-diversity values across taxonomic groups at the plot level (either including all taxonomic groups or only aboveground and belowground taxonomic groups).

In a recent development, we used the ANOVA type II test to assess the influence of land use on α- and β-multidiversity. In addition, we used ANOVA type III to evaluate the influence of land use, compartment (aboveground and belowground), and their interaction. This analysis was implemented in the car package103. We checked for normality and homogeneity of variance of residuals using the Shapiro–Wilk test and Levene’s test for homogeneity of variance. Further, we tested statistical pairwise differences using multiple comparisons of means with Tukey, with P values adjusted with the false discovery rate—that is, the expected proportion of false discoveries amongst the rejected hypotheses104—using the p.adjust function (fdr) in the stats R package.

For each taxon, we determined significant differences in diversity (α or β) of the current land use compared with the forest by calculating log ratio and 95% adjusted bootstrap confidence intervals as follows:.

It has been revealed that where ‘agricultural land use’ is the diversity value in the agricultural land use and ‘\(\overline{\mathrm{forest}}\)’ is the mean of the diversity in the forest. Negative and positive values indicate decreases and increases in diversity compared to the forest, respectively. For α-diversity, a pseudocount of 1 was added to all species count values to handle zeros while symmetrically preserving relative differences for count-like data—that is, \(\log [({\rm{a}}{\rm{g}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{c}}{\rm{u}}{\rm{l}}{\rm{t}}{\rm{u}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{l}}\,{\rm{l}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{n}}{\rm{d}}\,{\rm{u}}{\rm{s}}{\rm{e}}+1)/(\bar{{\rm{f}}{\rm{o}}{\rm{r}}{\rm{e}}{\rm{s}}{\rm{t}}}+1)]\). In the case of turnover and nestedness (0–1-scaled data), zeros were handled by adding 50% of the minimum non-zero value prior to log ratio calculation105, specifically, a pseudocount of 0.0357 was added for turnover (minimum non-zero value = 0.0714) and 0.00256 was added for nestedness (minimum non-zero value = 0.0051). We then calculated 95% confidence intervals for the log ratio using 10,000 bootstrap replicates (R package boot106, adjusted percentile bootstrap (bca-type)). If the 95% confidence intervals did not include zero, this indicated a significant difference between land use and the forest. As the results for diversity changes were largely consistent across q0 and q1 (Supplementary Fig. 9), we only show the results for q0. In addition, we performed t-tests to assess for significant differences between the log ratio and zero (forests as a reference), adjusting the P values using the false discovery rate (Supplementary Results).

Sources indicate that we calculated Pearson’s correlation with false discovery rate correction for species richness and pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity indices between each taxonomic group, irrespective of land-use type. The correlations are displayed in Supplementary Fig. 5.

Recent findings suggest that dissimilarities between pairwise observations were calculated separately for each taxonomic group and land use. Pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity was calculated using vegdist function (method = jaccard and binary = TRUE) in the R package vegan102,107. Afterward, we calculated mean pairwise dissimilarities for each site combination across all taxa. We then visualized the patterns in community composition using a non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) analysis of the mean pairwise dissimilarities for each plot combination. We used the envfit function from the R package vegan102,107 to fit environmental vectors onto the ordination of dissimilarities. The resulting plot coordinates on the NMDS scale were grouped by land-use type. In addition, significant differences among land uses were tested using an analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) on the pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity matrix using the ANOSIM function (permutations = 9999) from the R package vegan102,107. To test whether land use had an effect at the ecosystem level, including biotic and abiotic variables, we ran a multiple factor analysis. This analysis enables the identification of a common structure across two or more data matrices without assuming causation44, with canonical ordination methods being among the most powerful approaches for testing ecological relationships in a multivariate context44. To quantify the overall similarity (matrix correlation) between taxonomic groups in the multiple factor analysis, we used the RV coefficient, where 0 indicates no similarity and 1 indicates perfect similarity (Supplementary Table 1). We implemented this additional metric to test the robustness of our conclusions.

A GDM model was applied to each taxonomic group. We used the respective species matrix, the selected principal components for each group of environmental variables (see the section ‘Environmental data’), and the geographic plot coordinates to run the model. The execution of the GDM was performed using the gdm R package108. The contributions of environmental variables (principal components; Extended Data Fig. 7) and distance were estimated by extracting the maximum spline values (Supplementary Table 3). Significance testing of variables was performed using Monte Carlo sampling, implemented in the gdm.varImp function, with 250 permutations (Supplementary Table 2). All the analyses were performed in R v4.5.1 (ref. 109).

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data for the statistical analyses and main figures are stored in a Figshare repository (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31784410 (ref. 110)). Recorded (morpho-)species across taxa for canopy and leaf litter arthropods, butterflies, mesostigmatid mites and oribatid mites are deposited in the Ecotaxonomy database (http://ecotaxonomy.org). For birds, the automated sound recordings were uploaded to ecoSound-web (https://ecosound-web.de/ecosound_web/). Aural detections were confirmed with cross-checks on the Xeno-Canto online bird call database (http://xeno-canto.org/). Fungi have been deposited in the Dryad repository (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.7h44j0zrd (ref. 82)).

Code for the statistical analyses and main figures are available in a Figshare repository (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31784410 (ref. 110)).

#72514. Danny Drinkwater on Chelsea move he ‘could never turn down’

Danny Drinkwater on Chelsea move he ‘could never turn down’

📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (649 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readchelsea

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Danny Drinkwater Chelsea story still carries a sting.
  • Recent findings suggest that drinkwater opened up in a Truth or Padel appearance alongside David Ornstein.
  • Strip away the headlines and the numbers alone tell an uncomfortable story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Danny Drinkwater Chelsea story still carries a sting. Five years at Stamford Bridge gave him plenty of time to think about how it all turned out, and his own verdict is not a happy one.

Recent findings suggest that drinkwater opened up in a Truth or Padel appearance alongside David Ornstein. He noted the move was one he could never have turned down, even with the benefit of hindsight. “No, I don’t regret moving. I regret, in hindsight, how it’s turned out. I think I could never turn it down,” he said.

Strip away the headlines and the numbers alone tell an uncomfortable story. Drinkwater spent five years on Chelsea’s books. In that time he made just 23 appearances, according to the original interview report.

Do the maths and it barely comes to five games a year. That is a thin return for a central midfielder signed to compete for a first-team place. It is also the kind of record that rarely sits well at a club of Chelsea’s size and ambition.

Chelsea’s best attacking spells over a similar stretch of seasons look far more productive, as our striker rankings show. Set next to those numbers, Drinkwater’s five quiet years stand out even more starkly.

It has been revealed that five years. Twenty three games. These numbers alone explains why this transfer still gets talked about by Drinkwater, long after the headlines faded.

Sources indicate that the numbers only tell part of the story. A string of incidents turned a quiet, underwhelming spell into something far more pointed.

Recent findings suggest that drinkwater had a training-ground bust-up while out on loan. He was also involved in an on-pitch brawl with Chelsea’s own under-23s side. Flashpoints between a first-team player and a development squad are rare at any club, let alone one with Chelsea’s standards.

Taken alone, either incident might have passed as a bad day. Taken together, it became harder to see Drinkwater simply as an unlucky squad player who could not catch a break.

The most serious moment came during his time at Aston Villa. Drinkwater headbutted team-mate Jota and was fined two weeks’ wages for it. He indicates the consequences at Chelsea did not stop there.

“They didn’t formally ban me, but I got removed from the first team building after the incident at Villa,” Drinkwater stated.

One off-field incident, at another club, pushed him out of the manager’s day-to-day intends back home. No formal punishment at Chelsea followed. The effect was much the same.

Chelsea fans saw a similar breakdown of trust play out when Graham Potter struggled to win over the dressing room during another difficult Chelsea transition. Trust can break down fast once results or behaviour turn against the person at the centre of it.

Drinkwater’s comments matter beyond his own career. They are a reminder that saying yes to a big move does not guarantee it will work once a player walks through the door.

That tension has not gone away. Chelsea’s current transfer business, covered in our transfer watch, indicates the club still weighing big calls on players whose futures depend on more than form alone.

Squad management under Xabi Alonso, assessed in our bomb squad verdict, raises a familiar issue. Players who fall outside a manager’s plans rarely find a quick way back in, whether the exile is formal or not.

Drinkwater never found his way back into Chelsea’s plans after the Villa incident. His account of the Danny Drinkwater Chelsea years stands as a blunt warning. A move that looks impossible to refuse can still become one of the hardest spells of a career.

#72513. Bruno Fernandes breaks silence on Man Utd contract offer

Bruno Fernandes breaks silence on Man Utd contract offer

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readmanutd

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bruno Fernandes has been Manchester United’s most creative player since his arrival to the club in 2020.
  • The 32-year-old is approaching the final months of his current deal, which expires at the end of the season.
  • While they can extend his contract for a year, Manchester United are actively pursuing a deal to tie Bruno Fernandes beyond 2028.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bruno Fernandes has been Manchester United’s most creative player since his arrival to the club in 2020.

The 32-year-old is approaching the final months of his current deal, which expires at the end of the season. United do have the option to extend his contract by another 12 months, keeping him at Old Trafford until 2028.

While they can extend his contract for a year, Manchester United are actively pursuing a deal to tie Bruno Fernandes beyond 2028.

Bruno Fernandes himself has now confirmed that the club have offered him a latest contract, but the midfielder has made it clear that he does not want discussions about his future to become a priority right now.

Fernandes confirmed that an offer had been made but dismissed suggestions that he was holding out for a better salary or a longer agreement.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he told Sky Sports.

He also insisted that money has never been the reason behind his decision to remain at United, despite having opportunities to move elsewhere in previous transfer windows.

“If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here,” Fernandes stated.

The Portugal international added that he could have earned considerably more by accepting offers from other clubs, but always chose to continue his career in Manchester.

Fernandes revealed that discussions initially took place towards the end of last season and continued when the players returned for pre-season.

However, the United captain believes the current situation at the club makes it the wrong time to focus on his personal future.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side,” he explained.

“I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.”.

Industry observers note that fernandes has been one of United’s most influential players since arriving from Sporting in 2020. He has scored 75 Premier League goals for the club and set a new competition record for assists in a single season last term.

In a recent development, bruno’s comments don’t sound like he is holding United hostage demanding more pay or refusing to sign a new one. The intention as told by Bruno Fernandes just show his leadership trait about putting the team first. He has no immediate intention of making his contract situation the centre of attention. That will be a sign of encouragement for the fans as well.

Manchester United need to start winning games again. When they do and surely Bruno Fernandes will be at the centre of it, the contract talks can resume and take priority.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend with a growing treatment table and a lot of questions for Xabi Alonso to answer before Saturday’s visit of Bournemouth.

According to recent reports, the main concern revolves around Joao Pedro. Chelsea’s current player of the season rescued a point against newly promoted Hull, but he suffered a knock and sat out the damaging 3-0 defeat at Brentford. The problem also prompted his removal from Brazil’s squad shortly after he had returned to it.

It has been revealed that it is understood that he is undergoing specialist knee treatment in an attempt to expedite his recovery, although reports in Brazil suggest that he could be out for up to four weeks. No date has yet been set, but a return later in October looks most likely.

It has been revealed that there is more good news elsewhere. Cole Palmer was among the players called up to the latest England squad, which did not go down too well with Thomas Tuchel.

The midfielder has been recovering from a persistent groin injury and has been working with a rehab coach. He is likely to be fit this weekend.

It has been revealed that moises Caicedo has also struggled with an injury this season, playing just 14 minutes across the campaign. He’s spent the majority of time on the bench recovering from a bad calf injury, which ruled him out for most of the season.

He made his only appearance as a substitute against his former club Brighton, but the game was red-flagged for Ecuador’s friendlies, so he did not play.

It has been revealed that alonso mentioned before the Brentford match that the player would be ready to return. It seems to be the case, unless something went wrong.

According to recent reports, captain Reece James missed the Brentford game with yet another hamstring problem. Alonso mentioned he only just missed out, so a return seems likely.

According to recent reports, there may also be debuts. Marco Palestra, the £27m signing from Atalanta, has been sidelined since a training injury just before the opening match against Fulham. He is back in full training and was expected to feature in a behind-closed-doors friendly with Portsmouth. Chelsea lost 2-0. Emmanuel Emegha, injured after scoring against Bromley in July, is also pushing for involvement.

Less clear is the position of Jamie Gittens. He limped off with an ankle injury playing for England Under-21s against Kazakhstan and was seen on crutches. Mike Penders is fine after a quad scare on Belgium duty. Returning to the bench against Turkey.

Chelsea badly need a lift. Defeat at Brentford before the break left Alonso’s side looking shaky, and a squad stretched by injuries has not helped.

Saturday brings a chance to steady things. If Palmer, James and Caicedo are available, with Palestra and Emegha potentially adding fresh options, the picture will look much brighter at Stamford Bridge. Joao Pedro’s absence will still sting. However, a strong response against Bournemouth would go a long way towards easing the pressure and restoring belief.

Liverpool v Manchester United: Five classic wins at Anfield

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With Mauricio Pochettino preparing for his first match in charge against Liverpool on Sunday, we look back at five occasions when United emerged victorious from one of English football’s fiercest fixtures.
  • Industry observers note that united travelled to Anfield on 19 April 1997 knowing Liverpool could overtake them at the top of the Premier League with a victory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Diego Forlan’s unforgettable double to Juan Mata’s spectacular volley, Manchester United have enjoyed some memorable victories at Anfield over the years.

With Mauricio Pochettino preparing for his first match in charge against Liverpool on Sunday, we look back at five occasions when United emerged victorious from one of English football’s fiercest fixtures.

Industry observers note that united travelled to Anfield on 19 April 1997 knowing Liverpool could overtake them at the top of the Premier League with a victory. Instead, centre-back Gary Pallister scored twice with headers from David Beckham deliveries, either side of John Barnes’s equaliser.

In a recent development, andy Cole added a third after the interval, heading home from Gary Neville’s cross following an error by Liverpool goalkeeper David James. The victory helped Sir Alex Ferguson’s side take a decisive step towards retaining the Premier League title, which they secured the following month.

It has been revealed that fresh from winning the Treble, United returned to Anfield for a remarkable match in September 1999. Jamie Carragher headed into his own net inside three minutes before Andy Cole doubled United’s advantage.

Sami Hyypia pulled a goal back for Liverpool, but Carragher’s second own goal restored the visitors’ two-goal lead. Patrik Berger reduced the deficit again, and United faced a difficult finish after Cole was sent off for a second bookable offence. Despite playing the closing stages with 10 men, Ferguson’s side held on for a 3-2 victory.

According to recent reports, diego Forlan had endured a frustrating start to his United career before producing a performance that supporters would remember for years. The Uruguayan opened the scoring after Liverpool goalkeeper Jerzy Dudek failed to gather the ball, allowing him to finish from close range.

In a recent development, forlan added a second just minutes later, beating Dudek at his near post to put United in control. Sami Hyypia pulled one back for Liverpool, but Ferguson’s side held on for a victory that proved valuable in their successful pursuit of the 2002-03 Premier League title. Forlan’s double also inspired a terrace song that remains familiar to United supporters.

Few United victories at Anfield have been as dramatic as the one secured by John O’Shea in March 2007. Liverpool had enjoyed the better opportunities, and United’s task became harder when Paul Scholes was sent off late in the second half.

Industry observers note that with a goalless draw appearing increasingly likely, Cristiano Ronaldo’s free-kick was parried by goalkeeper Pepe Reina. Substitute O’Shea reacted quickest, firing the rebound high into the net in stoppage time. The unexpected winner gave United three valuable points on their way to reclaiming the Premier League title.

Juan Mata produced one of the most memorable individual performances in this fixture during Louis van Gaal’s first season as United manager. The Spaniard opened the scoring after 14 minutes, finishing a move involving Ander Herrera, before doubling United’s lead with a spectacular scissor-kick volley after half-time.

Recent findings suggest that liverpool captain Steven Gerrard had been sent off just 38 seconds after coming on as a substitute at the interval. Daniel Sturridge reduced the deficit, while Wayne Rooney missed a late penalty, but United held on for a 2-1 victory. Mata’s second goal remains one of the outstanding moments of United’s Premier League visits to Anfield.

Those five victories underline the different ways United have succeeded at Anfield, from outstanding individual performances to late winners and determined defensive displays. Pochettino now has an opportunity to begin his managerial reign with a memorable result against United’s biggest rivals.

Which United victory at Anfield is your favourite? Were you there for Forlan’s double, O’Shea’s winner or Mata’s volley? Share your memories in the comments below.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club opting to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.
  • The departure is understood to be amicable and won’t take immediate effect.
  • The story was first reported by Matt Law of The Telegraph and Nizaar Kinsella of BBC Sport, with Ben Jacobs subsequently providing further details about how Chelsea intend to operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club opting to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.

The departure is understood to be amicable and won’t take immediate effect. Stewart could continue attending matches before formally leaving, following discussions with co-owner Behdad Eghbali over the club’s evolving sporting structure.

The story was first reported by Matt Law of The Telegraph and Nizaar Kinsella of BBC Sport, with Ben Jacobs subsequently providing further details about how Chelsea intend to operate.

Stewart arrived from Monaco in October 2022 as technical director before becoming co-sporting director alongside Paul Winstanley in February 2023.

Chelsea’s day-to-day sporting leadership will now be shared between Winstanley, Sam Jewell and Joe Shields, each with defined responsibilities.

Winstanley will continue overseeing transfer negotiations, player contracts and several departments at Cobham, including medical and performance operations. Shields’ work centres on the academy and player pathways, while Jewell has wider responsibilities across the BlueCo operation, including Strasbourg.

According to Jacobs, discussions about restructuring began in April and accelerated following the appointment of Xabi Alonso as head coach.

Stewart had overseen investment in Chelsea’s data analysis operation, although Jewell and Shields have increasingly taken responsibility for using that information in recruitment and talent identification.

Dave Fallows will remain involved in an advisory capacity, rather than taking on a fixed day-to-day portfolio.

The changes are being described as a natural evolution of Chelsea’s sporting model. There is no suggestion that Stewart’s departure followed a breakdown in relations, and the club are not at the moment planning to recruit a replacement.

There will be no live UK television coverage of Chelsea’s return to Premier League action against Bournemouth on Saturday afternoon.

Xabi Alonso’s side host the Cherries at Stamford Bridge in a traditional 3pm kick-off, with the fixture falling within the Saturday afternoon broadcasting blackout.

That means supporters unable to attend will need to follow the match through other channels, rather than watching it live on Sky Sports or TNT Sports.

Although the game will not be televised live in the UK, supporters can follow developments through the official Chelsea website and the Premier League website.

The Saturday 3pm blackout prevents live domestic television broadcasts during the restricted period, although overseas coverage may be available through broadcasters holding the relevant rights.

Highlights will be available after the match through the usual broadcast and digital channels, subject to their respective release schedules.

Chelsea will then turn their attention to a trip to Everton on Saturday, 17 October, with that fixture scheduled for a 12.30pm kick-off at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

For Alonso, the Bournemouth match provides the immediate opportunity to resume Chelsea’s domestic campaign following the international break.

Bournemouth’s determination to keep Alex Scott has done little to discourage Chelsea, who remain among the leading contenders to sign the England midfielder.

It has been revealed that the Blues had a £64m bid rejected during the summer, but their interest has continued into the new season. According to Matt Law of The Telegraph, Chelsea are at the front of the queue of clubs monitoring the 23-year-old.

Sources indicate that bournemouth, however, have no intention of allowing Scott to leave in January. talkSPORT reported this week that the south coast club remain determined to retain him, despite his reluctance to sign a contract extension.

Scott’s current deal runs until 2028, leaving Bournemouth with time to negotiate, although their position could become more complicated if no agreement is reached before next summer.

The midfielder’s immediate priority is recovering from a thigh injury sustained while representing England. He impressed during the 7-0 Nations League victory over Croatia but was withdrawn after 70 minutes. Subsequent examinations revealed a quadriceps problem, with BBC Sport reporting that he could miss six to eight weeks.

His absence is a setback for Bournemouth, who have relied heavily on the former Bristol City midfielder this season. It also introduces another consideration for clubs monitoring his progress ahead of the January window.

Chelsea are not alone in their admiration. Arsenal and Liverpool have also been linked with Scott, whose performances have attracted attention beyond the Premier League.

Suggestions circulating on social media that Bournemouth have already agreed to let him leave in January remain unsubstantiated. There has been no reliable confirmation of such an arrangement, and the club’s reported position is firmly against a winter sale.

For Chelsea, the more realistic opportunity may come next summer, particularly if Scott continues to resist signing a new contract.

  • Here is our 7pm round-up of the latest Chelsea news for Thursday, 8 October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea’s sporting department is facing another change following news of Laurence Stewart’s impending departure, while the club continue to be linked with potential additions to their squad.

Alex Scott and Palmeiras teenager Eduardo Conceicao have both featured in Thursday’s transfer coverage, with Xabi Alonso also preparing his players for Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth.

Here is our 7pm round-up of the latest Chelsea news for Thursday, 8 October.

Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club planning to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.

His departure is understood to be amicable and will not take immediate effect. Stewart joined from Monaco in 2022, initially as technical director, before becoming co-sporting director alongside Paul Winstanley.

As detailed in our report on Stewart’s departure and Chelsea’s leadership reshuffle, Winstanley, Sam Jewell and Joe Shields are expected to take on expanded responsibilities across recruitment, player development and the wider BlueCo operation.

According to recent reports, the changes follow discussions about the club’s sporting structure that reportedly began earlier this year. There is no confirmed suggestion that Stewart’s departure resulted from a disagreement with Alonso.

Chelsea’s reported interest in Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott remains a talking point, despite the south coast club’s determination to retain the England international.

The Blues reportedly had a £64m offer rejected during the summer, with Matt Law of The Telegraph subsequently identifying Chelsea as leading contenders for the 23-year-old.

However, as examined in our latest report on Chelsea’s interest in Scott, Bournemouth are not expected to entertain a January sale.

Industry observers note that scott’s immediate concern is recovering from a thigh injury suffered while representing England. The midfielder could face several weeks on the sidelines, potentially complicating Bournemouth’s plans as well as any future discussions about his next move.

Chelsea have also reportedly made contact with Palmeiras over 16-year-old forward Eduardo Conceicao, who is attracting attention from several leading European clubs.

According to Mark Brus of CaughtOffside, Chelsea have held discussions with the Brazilian club as they explore the possibility of a future deal.

Our report on Chelsea’s interest in Eduardo Conceicao explains that a valuation as high as €100m has been suggested, although that figure is not a confirmed asking price or evidence of a formal bid.

Manchester City, Arsenal and Real Madrid are among the other clubs reportedly monitoring the teenager. Conceicao would be unable to complete a transfer to England until he turns 18, making any prospective move a longer-term consideration.

Alonso’s attention will now turn to Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge.

The match kicks off at 3pm and will not be televised live in the United Kingdom because of the Saturday afternoon broadcasting blackout.

Our Chelsea v Bournemouth kick-off and how-to-watch guide provides the full details, including how to follow the match and the available overseas broadcast information.

Scott’s injury is expected to deprive Bournemouth of an important midfield option, although Chelsea will have their own fitness decisions to make as players return from international duty.

Sources indicate that after Saturday’s fixture, Chelsea travel to Hill Dickinson Stadium to face Everton on 17 October. Alonso will be looking for greater consistency as the domestic programme resumes.

#72502. Pressing with intensity, getting runners beyond Kane and playing like a 'Premier League team': How Thomas Tuchel's newly introduced-look England dismantled Spain - and what he's learned from cowardly retreat against Argentina

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1615 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

Pressing with intensity, getting runners beyond Kane and playing like a 'Premier League team': How Thomas Tuchel's newly introduced-look England dismantled Spain - and what he's learned from cowardly retreat against Argentina

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:59 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 12:59 EST, 16 November 2026.
  • By the end of the World Cup, it felt as if Argentina had ripped the mask off Thomas Tuchel’s England only to reveal Gareth Southgate’s England standing there blinking right back at them.
  • On the biggest stage, against the biggest teams, under the biggest pressure, England wilted as they always did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 12:59 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 12:59 EST, 16 November 2026.

By the end of the World Cup, it felt as if Argentina had ripped the mask off Thomas Tuchel’s England only to reveal Gareth Southgate’s England standing there blinking right back at them.

On the biggest stage, against the biggest teams, under the biggest pressure, England wilted as they always did. They sat back, they were too cautious, and they lost. And yet, ever since, Tuchel has turned England into a free-scoring winning machine, topped off by a famous victory in Madrid, ending Spain’s 43-match unbeaten streak.

In the six games since the summer, England have scored 19 goals and conceded six. Five of those have been against the world champions.

Yes, this was the Nations League and not a World Cup semi-final. No, it wasn’t at the end of a gruelling five weeks of heat, humidity and altitude. And, yes, it was only a terrific late double save from James Trafford that stopped this being yet another tale of self-sabotaging England, thanks to Elliot Anderson’s red card, blowing another lead when under pressure.

In a recent development, but, this time, England did see it out. They secured Tuchel’s biggest win as England boss and, in doing so, showed us just how he’s been able to get his side playing his way.

Harry Kane leads the England celebrations after his side's victory over Spain in Madrid on Sunday night.

Remember when everyone used to lose their minds whenever Harry Kane dropped deep in big games under Southgate? He’s our bloody striker, for goodness sake. Get in the box!

After England’s defeat by Spain in the Euro 2024 final two years ago, Opta posted on X that Kane had touched the ball just once in the opposition box across both that game and their previous final heartbreak against Italy three years earlier.

It has been revealed that ‘One fewer than Jack Grealish,’ the post continued. ‘Grealish played 21 minutes in the 2020 final and didn't make the Euro 2024 squad.’.

Recent findings suggest that ballon d’Or winner Kane has made it quite clear since that he doesn’t need to spend all his time in the box to influence games. When he drops deeper, Kane is able to show the full extent of his creativity and range of passing.

The main problem with the ploy under Southgate, however, was that Kane rarely had the team-mates to make the right runs ahead of him. He was surrounded by players who wanted to take up similar positions. Just look at the average position maps (below) from England’s loss to Spain at Euro 2024 compared to last night.

The average position map of England’s players in the loss to Spain at Euro 2024 show how Kane dropped deep, without team-mates making runs for him to exploit.

...whereas on Sunday night he had runners - Anthony Gordon, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers - around and beyond him.

Two years ago, the only player who averaged their touches ahead of Kane was Bukayo Saka. Jude Bellingham was out wide. Kobbie Mainoo and Phil Foden were basically in Kane’s shadow.

On Sunday night, he had Anthony Gordon, the brilliant, belligerent Bellingham and Morgan Rogers all ahead of him – and nearly even Ben White.

That desire, and instruction, to flock forward under Tuchel has made such a difference.

Recent findings suggest that take England’s third goal (below). Kane has the ball outside the area. Rogers is bombing on to his left. Gordon, who started as a winger but finds himself occupying the central spaces Kane leaves behind, darts into the box and points to where he wants it.

Bellingham is demanding the ball, too, showing Kane he wants it to feet. Even Anderson is charging into the box. Kane finds Bellingham, who feeds the unseen White, sprinting forward on the overlap to finish.

Kane picks up the ball and is met with an array of options in front of him, ahead of England's third goal.

He did similar in the win against Croatia a few days earlier, too.

Kane collects the ball deep with four bodies ahead of him, including full backs Lewis Hall and Trent Alexander-Arnold.

It his raking pass to the back post which allows Bellingham to set up Rogers to finish.

Kane's lofted pass to Rogers (top right) leads to a goal against Croatia for Bellingham (edge of box).

In a recent development, england’s fluidity in the final third is bamboozling defences. That is how you get the best of Kane’s creativity.

PLAYING LIKE A PREMIER LEAGUE SIDE.

Football is changing, so Pep Guardiola told us all in January last year. The modern game is now how teams like Bournemouth and Brighton play. The current Premier League table would suggest he had a point.

Over the past few years in the English top flight, we have seen teams move away from an obsession with keeping the ball for the sake of it and turn towards a far faster, more aggressive and more physical style of play.

Sources indicate that tuchel wants to take from that playbook. ‘We're at our best when we're free, physically overpowering and making it Premier League-level,’ said Kane after last month's 7-0 rout of Croatia.

In the six matches since the World Cup, Tuchel’s England are having much less of the ball than they did at the start of his reign – and now less even than under Southgate.

Industry observers note that the key is they are becoming ever more direct with it. Tuchel wants his England to play out of the back with short passes, entice opponents on to them, but then move it through the lines at speed.

Recent findings suggest that since the World Cup, England are playing far fewer passes, but more of them into the box – to find those runners. A higher percentage of them forward. More direct attacks, moving the ball up the field at a quicker speed.

On Sunday night, they revealed how Tuchel wants his side to press. ‘We were hungry in the opposition half,’ mentioned the England boss at full time.

Industry observers note that A fine example of that (below) came just after just six minutes. Declan Rice gives his Arsenal team-mate Martín Zubimendi no time at all on the ball inside his own area, charging him down, and forcing him to play out to another Gunner in Mikel Merino. But he, too, is being harassed by Anderson and eventually England win it back and set up Kane for a chance that he fizzes wide.

A half-fit Rice was unable to apply that pressure in the summer.

Declan Rice charges forward to close down Martin Zubimendi who has possession just inside the Spanish box with Kane and Bellingham already engaged in a high press...

...Zubimendi passes to Mikel Merino but Elliot Anderson is all over him and it leads to Kane shot that just fizzes wide.

So much of this improvement under Tuchel into a side capable of blowing teams away can be put down to another abstract word he used post-match in Madrid: ‘brave’.

Tuchel talked in the last international break of ‘unlocking the next level’, and taking ‘calculated risks’ with a ‘man-to-man’ press in the opposition half.

Under Southgate, and certainly in the cowardly retreat against Argentina in the summer, England demonstrated little bravery either with the ball or without it and frequently showed too much respect to those big nations.

Too safe with the ball, too afraid to give it away, and too fearful to try to win it back in case you leave yourself open.

That appears to be changing, too. There was a moment at the start of the second half when Bellingham tried a risky through-ball to Rogers, which failed to find its man, instead of another simple ball out wide.

It handed Spain possession cheaply. But England didn’t care because they just pounced again. Spain couldn’t deal with it. In the first half, Spain completed just 84 per cent of their passes in their own half – a place where they are usually able to knock it about at will – their lowest completion rate according to Opta since the 2010 World Cup. They didn’t have a shot on target until the penalty.

England’s defence has long been seen as the weak spot and, under Southgate, it felt as though he always would rather his attacking talents not be too frivolous for fear of exposing it.

Thomas Tuchel and Kane direct England's players to keep on the front foot during the win over Spain.

According to recent reports, tuchel is doing the opposite. England’s expected goals soared from 1.7 per game under Southgate from the 2022 World Cup to the end of his reign, to 2.2 under Tuchel’s until this summer’s tournament. Since then, it’s jumped again to 2.8 but at the cost of what they are conceding. In his early days, England coughed up fewer good chances than under Southgate but since the World Cup has more than doubled.

He will want to get that down, of course, but when you are creating so much – and have an array of top finishers to see them off – how much will that matter to Tuchel?

According to recent reports, even he’s getting braver. His decision to take off Gordon for Konsa and chuck as many defenders on during England’s shrinking against Argentina looked a decision that would forever haunt Tuchel’s tenure.

It has been revealed that against Spain, Kane made way but Tuchel ended the game with striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin on the pitch. Against Spain, he held his nerve.

In a recent development, west Ham’s veteran midfielder has been the subject of an honest interview in his home country on Czech radio coinciding with the release of his autobiography. One of the more revealing comments Tomas Soucek made concerns the pressure and the expectation of playing in front of a major audience – such as West Ham will undoubtedly face tomorrow as the season re-commences with a home tie at London Stadium in front of 60,000 expectant supporters.

It has been revealed that unlike several others, from his words it is clear that Soucek seems to thrive on the pressure and the weight of expectation upon him. As one of only a handful of medal winners still at the club from the 2023 campaign, Soucek’s experience should become a steadying influence in the dressing room even though he mostly starts games on the bench these days.

Handling the weight of expectation at London Stadium has been daunting at times.

‘Tornado Tom’ reveals that, far from letting it get to him, he actually enjoys the weight of expectation and pressure :.

“Yes, obviously I feel it, but I like the pressure. Because football is always up and down, you have so many wins and so many losses – and it’s up to you how you recover from all of it.

“And I love that. As you stated, it’s the most watched league in the world. And West Ham’s fans are crazy – they’re the best in the league, and it’s such a historic club.

“From the first day until now, I think me and West Ham connection is as good as it could possibly be in all aspects.

“And, yes, the pressure is there, but I try to work with it – and that’s why we play football.” (englishradio.cz).

The pressure will be significantly eased with a clean sheet and three points tomorrow – whether Soucek now, 31 gets into the action or simply acts as a calming figure in the dressing room. He is one of those very rare characters in the West Ham team – a leader on and off the pitch – and in another era could have spent years as the club’s captain.
